subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, July 2, consideration of Bill C-8, to establish a national petroleum company, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, and motion No. 4 (Mr. Stevens).

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment yesterday I was discussing the amendment to Bill C-8, which, of course, is to establish a national petroleum company, Petro-Can. The amendment is to clause 22, which briefly provides that the government may advance money out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by way of loans for the financing of Petro-Can, such advance to be free of interest. If I may put the amendment on the record, it is to amend clause 22 in the following way:
-by striking out line 34 at page 15 and substituting therefor the following:
"determine,
and any amount so advanced by way of loan on purchase shall bear interest at a rate that is not less than the rate approved by the Minister of Finance for that quarter of the year in which such amount is advanced as the standard rate of interest for loans to Crown corporations that are repayable within a period not exceeding twelve months."
Having heard the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) move the amendment last night, I then listened to the minister, who of course opposed the amendment. He took the position that Petro-Can should have a favoured and privileged position in that money should be advanced to it out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund-which is taxpayers' money-without interest. As I said last night, I am going to speak in favour of the hon. member's amendment.
This bill seeks to advance to Petro-Can $1.5 billion of taxpayers' money by way of loan free of interest. I was rather shocked last night to hear the minister, in opposing the amendment, say that private corporations do not pay interest on money advanced on the purchase of shares. Although this is correct, money that is advanced to any private corporation, in the oil business or in any other business, must bear the going rate of interest. The minister ought to know that in many cases money raised by the sale of shares is but a small portion of the capital required by a company for the purpose of exploration and development, in this business or any other.
The private sector raises money by dividends, bonds and debentures. On that money, the going market rate of interest must be paid. In many cases today, as I am sure the minister, who should have some knowledge of business, knows, companies in the oil business are forced to pay a higher rate of interest because they are competing with other endeavours in which the risk is less. Therefore, my first question is: Why the discrimination in this case? Why should this company be put in a favoured position and get capital from the people of Canada without payment of any interest at all? This company will be a charge upon the taxpayers of Canada.
It was my understanding from listening to what the minister said in committee that Petro-Can was being set up as a Crown corporation for two reasons, and I think it is essential that we examine those two reasons in view of the fact that we are advancing such a large sum of money. The minister's first reason for setting up this company, outside of his liking for statism, is to encourage exploration and development. His second reason is to assure that the price of gasoline to the consumers of Canada is kept down.
I guess a third reason which he gave is that the resource industry is foreign-owned and controlled. I think there is a mistake in the thinking of a lot of people in this regard. When a corporation drills a well, whether a gas well or an oil well, it drills on leased land, land that is owned by the Crown and that is subject to regulations and rules contained in the leases. So, in fact, none of these private or international companies ever really control the resources of Canada in the sense of owning them. They may be able to make agreements with the Crown, but as we have seen over the last two years both the federal government and some provincial governments have torn up contracts existing between the Crown and the business community and have started all over again. Their security of tenure is not very great as far as these leases are concerned.
One must ask himself immediately what effect this interest-free money in the amount of $1.5 billion will have on the objectives of the minister. Let us deal with the first objective, to encourage and stimulate exploration and development. It would appear now that the great new fields to be found in Canada are in the north and Petro-Can, a taxpayers' liability, will be asked to compete against the private sector which is forced to pay high rates of interest, partly due to the policies of this government. Hence the long-term picture in my opinion will be one of discouragement to the private sector from the continuation of exploration and development in Canada because of the unfair and unreasonable cost of risk capital to them in competing against a company that does not have to pay any interest on this amount of $1.5 billion. The uncertainty created and the disadvantages imposed on the private

Petro-Canada
sector by this and other legislation will, in the very near future, destroy Canada's favourable position of being the only nation in the western world self-sufficient in petroleum and natural gas. Incidentally, I might say that this self-sufficiency has occurred in less than 30 years because at one time we imported about 95 per cent to 96 per cent of our oil and other energy sources.
It is beyond me to imagine how the government could develop such negative thinking. This government, like many other governments, is blinded by statism and control and will do anything to devise any excuse to create new Crown corporation empires, many of which we have seen and were dealt with by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Many of these Crown corporations are inefficient, expensive and far from satisfactory. I want to emphasize that we are not dealing with ordinary commerce. We are not dealing with that kind of business, but rather we are dealing with a high-risk capital business. I said last night that Imperial Oil had drilled 133 dry holes before they struck oil which led to the discovery of the fields in Alberta and other parts of western Canada, which in turn gave us self-sufficiency.
We are dealing with high-risk capital and we are putting the taxpayers' money into this high-risk business. Apparently, we are to have Petro-Can. I should like to see the idea abandoned, and I do not know why the government is going ahead with it at this time of restraint. The government has said it is going to save $1 billion, and I suggest it could start off by saving $1.5 billion right away if it scrapped this idea. I make that suggestion because the government does not need this company. There are other vehicles. The minister has said the government is putting $300 million into Syncrude. Panarctic has done a pretty good job and we could take advantage of it.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I am glad that some of my friends in the Liberal party agree with me. I know that some of them disagree with some of their ministers in caucus, because these things leak out once in a while. It is beyond me to imagine how the majority of members over there can think in this way.
The second objective of Petro-Can, to be financed by taxpayers' money without interest, is to keep down the price of gasoline. That is a very interesting objective, to keep down the price of gasoline. The facts are, of course, that because of a tax policy of this government, and because we are dealing with risk capital which likely will be handled inefficiently, Petro-Can will manage to discourage the private sector from development and exploration. Once we lose our self-sufficiency and our security of supply, then gasoline will increase in price. The fact is that the government can and should be named right now the "gasoline buck-boys". It will not be very long before the cost of gasoline at the pumps or at the retail level will be $1 per gallon, and in some areas even higher, perhaps $1.50 a gallon. I sincerely suggest that gasoline will be as high as $1 a gallon throughout Canada by September or October of this year.
We have a situation now in which this government is asking us to advance $1.5 billion interest-free to a Crown corporation, and the same government has just come along

with a 10-cent a gallon tax on gasoline. This government is very kind to the consumer. It has also increased the price of crude oil by $1.50 a barrel. Last week I discussed the situation with some experts in Calgary, and I think it is fair to suggest that Calgary is the capital of the oil industry in Canada. These experts in the oil industry say they will be lucky, if, out of the $1.50 increase per barrel, they get 22 cents. They suggest the rest will go in taxes to the provincial treasuries or the federal treasury.
Taking into consideration this economic climate, together with the money to be advanced putting Petro-Can in a more favourable position, certainly exploration and development will not be encouraged. Without continued exploration and development, we will experience a short oil supply and up will go the price of gas, because then we must rely on the OPEC countries for our imports into Canada or their exports, whichever way you want it. Once we get into that position we will be in the same position as other countries, such as the United States, which is now spending about $30 billion a year, an amount greater than our entire budget, for the importation of crude petroleum and other forms of energy.
If one of the objectives of this company is to bring down the price of gas, that objective certainly is covered by a cloud of hypocrisy because the price of gas is on the rise now, not only as a result of other government economic programs but because of its program to discourage exploration and development. Let me make that point once again, because of its importance in terms of this amendment, As a result of giving Petro-Can $1.5 billion interest free and free of any charge, enabling it to compete with the private sector, which has to pay up to 9 per cent, 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent for its money, you will discourage exploration and development. By discouraging exploration and development, you place energy of this nature in short supply and up goes the price.
Not only does this company get this money tax free, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) has refused to produce regulations governing the leasing of land. I ask why this is the case. Spokesmen for this government say they do not want to draft regulations for this department because there are pools of oil and gas to be found in the north and the government wants the private sector to go in and start drilling. I suppose when the private sector finds a favoured field, the government will then pass these regulations, giving this interest-free company a favoured position in order that it can compete against the private sector.
Hon. members may say that sounds good because this will redound to the benefit of the taxpayers. There may be something to be said for that argument. From an academic point of view I can see some people buying that argument. What this will do is drive out the private sector. As a result, other fields will not be found and we will be back in short supply and the price of gasoline will go up again to every consumer in Canada. That is what we are talking about and it does not take much of an economist to figure that out, because the law of supply and demand always works, even when there are controls.
This government's policy is one of watch and wait. The private sector has the know-how and the expertise necessary to discover and find these fields of oil and gas. Once
July 3, 1975

they have done so, then the regulations will be shaped and trimmed to favour Petro-Can with all its interest-free money. Can anyone in his right mind believe that international companies will continue to find oil and gas, only to discover that Petro-Can will take over the fields?
One of the provinces in western Canada tried that and that is one reason Alberta today has about 86 per cent of the known and proved resources in this country. In the 1940's the drilling rigs left Saskatchewan because of a similar policy on the part of that government. It said to the industry that it should find the oil and gas and, if it did, it would then belong to the province. People just do not operate a business on that basis. Even if you tried this on a very small business you would run into the same difficulty. If you are selling hot dogs on the street, and as soon as you start making a profit somebody takes over the business you will find you just cannot do business on that basis. Can anybody in his right mind really believe that the international companies will continue to find oil for Canada on this basis?
This all adds up to one thing. If we are to remain self-sufficient, then the same rules that apply to the private sector must apply to Petro-Can. Why should Petro-Can be given a favoured position? How can the private sector operate in that kind of a climate? In my experience they can only do so on one basis, and this may be the strongest part of my argument. Because of the efficiency of the oil industry, even dealing in risk capital, the industry will out manoeuvre Petro-Can at every stage.
I am unequivocally opposed to Petro-Can, but if we are going to have it thrust on us by this government with the support of those socialists in the NDP, then let us have rules and regulations so that everybody is operating under the same rules, playing the same game. Imagine if you had a baseball league and you gave the Red Sox a different set of rules under which they played than you gave the other teams. This is in effect what you are asking. I suggest that you would soon have the other teams dropping out of the league, and that is what you are going to get from the private sector.
I have spoken longer than I intended to, but those are some of the reasons I support the amendment. I ask the minister and the government to reconsider their position about advancing this money without interest because other Crown corporations are asked to pay interest, except the CBC which borrows money when it has no assets with which to ever repay it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, when first conceived, of course was a bad bill. It is less evil now than it was in its original form. The fact of the matter, however, is that it is still considered to be wrong. It was conceptually wrong right from the outset. I think previous speakers have touched on the fact that the most serious damage that is being done by the introduction of the Petro-Can concept is the fact that the government is now entering into the petroleum game, but has decided not to play by the same rules as other companies in the private sector. It is a rather serious situation into which the government is entering, a situation wherein the government now enters the petroleum industry with spe-
Petro-Canada
cial and separate rules for itself. It has special rules in terms of the financial structure, in terms of its right to be able to drill for oil and in terms of its right to access to research related to the petroleum industry. All that of course leads to the essential problem which was enunciated with the concept of Petro-Can.
The problem is that we now have a Crown corporation entering into the field with a separate set of regulations for itself. This will cause a degree of trepidation in the private sector. It will certainly stir up and haunt the private people. It will tend to prevent any efficient search for supplies. There can be no genuine search for supplies in this country so long as the government is taking part in this kind of activity. This causes a degree of nervousness in the private sector. That is what is happening. So long as we have a nervous private sector, there will be no increase in supplies in this country. Anyone who analyzes what Petro-Can will do soon comes to the obvious conclusion that it is to be a company quite apart from our traditional companies. If it is to have a separate status there will be a ripple of fear throughout the whole industry. It is that ripple of fear that will damage this country. My argument will be that this will offset any gain that would ever come from the $l'/2 billion being spent by this government.
We might take a look at some of the arguments advanced in yesterday's debate on the amendments. As recorded at page 7200 of Hansard, we note that the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) quoted the petroleum industry as saying:
If we don't get more money we are going to slow down our exploration programs.
Then, he went on to say that the oil companies have been shifting their drilling rigs south of the border. Some members in the Progressive Conservative Party said, of course, that this will only happen if we destroy the profit motive because they will go where the profit is. Somehow the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands set the stage to assume that so long as these rigs went where there is a profit, there is something evil or harmful associated with it. What he failed to say was that to the south we have the United States which has no Crown corporations. They are telling us they want to be self-sufficient in energy by the mid-1980's. The fact of the matter is that that country uses far more energy than we do, possibly for no other reason than they have ten times the population we have. The private sector in the United States is moving. Advances are being made and they are talking about self-sufficiency.
Members opposite and members of the NDP have been trying to tell us what is happening in this search for supply. We might take a look at some of the illogical conclusions that have been drawn. I will again quote the same member. He said:
The real tragedy is that a national petroleum company was not set up 10 or 12 years ago.
Then, he continues with this statement:
How can the Canadian people participate in an industry 90 per cent of which is today controlled by foreign oil companies.
Well, if there is a fear about foreign ownership, that does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that therefore there ought to be a government-owned corporation. There

is no logic in the statement that because you do not like foreign ownership you should nationalize everything. You would adopt the same kind of logic if you were to say that because a duck can swim, then Donald is a good swimmer and therefore he is a duck. This kind of argument simply does not fit. Members of the government say there are some problems; they identify the problems and then come up with some kind of an answer without a connection between the stated problem and the projected solution. That is the kind of illogical thinking we have in this situation.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has told us in the House and the committee that he has been bombarded with questions that he has answered over and over again. If we take a look at some of the statements the minister has made, I think we can establish the fact that he simply does not answer the questions. On page 7,025 of Hansard, in response to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is recorded as stating:
... the hon. gentleman's amendment and speech are one of the areas where the technique in committee was to raise a question which would be responded to again and again, and still at the end the hon. member would claim that I had not replied to his question.
That was never the position of members of the opposition. We knew there were replies to the questions we were asking. We also know that the minister, in responding, never gave an answer. There is a difference between uttering words and giving logical reasons.
I might cite another example which adopts itself directly to the same situation. Again quoting from Hansard, the minister said that he wanted the members of Petro-Can to play by the same rules as the other companies in the private sector. I challenge the minister to tell us in this House the name of one private oil company that has received $1.5 billion of interest-free money. If Petro-Can is to play by the same rules, and that is his statement, then let him come forward and tell us the name of any oil company which has received interest-free money. Let him also share with us the name of any company that would be privileged to drill on land under the conditions explained by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) when he said that Petro-Can would have privileges and rights in respect of northern lands. Let him also explain the situation in respect of research whereby the government can collect all the results of the research conducted by the private companies for its drilling program.
If the minister cannot guarantee that the rules of the game are to be the same, then obviously there will be fear in the private sector and the whole object of establishing a national petroleum company, namely to increase supplies, will have the opposite result. A national petroleum company would not necessarily resolve the problems nor put right the evils which have been identified in the industry. There is no doubt that there is a need to increase the supply. The fact of the matter is that this can be documented fairly substantially. It is well known that exploration activities have lagged by 20 per cent in 1974. The production of Canadian crude was down 6 per cent in 1974 and dropped again another 11 per cent in 1975. On January 1 of 1974, there were 334 drilling rigs in Canada. That number has now been reduced to 235, a decline of 100 rigs

or 31 per cent. At the same time, Canada is no longer self-sufficient in oil. That, of course, is partly the premise upon which the government builds its argument for the establishment of a national petroleum company. However, what the government has never considered is the reason for the reduction. The petroleum industry has had a cash flow reduction of $500 million since 1974 due to taxes and royalties, making it impossible for them to raise the required money.
[DOT] (U30)
I think it is important to note the fact that Canada was the only country in the world with a petroleum potential to have shown a decline in activity in 1974 which demonstrates that the problem has not been only in the private sector. If we take a look at all the countries in the world with a petroleum potential we find that Canada was the only one to slow down and the only one to have had the intervention of government policies to such an extent that the private sector simply could not conclude whether the government was suffering from schizophrenia or paranoia. There was no way in which companies in the private sector could make predictions and long-term judgments, and that is necessary. People in the industry tell us that they can work on a narrow margin, but they have to be able to make long-term judgments. When you have rapid changes in policy, long-term judgments cannot be made. It is as a result of the impossibility of making long-term judgments that drilling rigs in the country were reduced in number and consequently exploration activities were reduced. So, the government caused the problem and now is trying to establish a motive for solving it in its own way.
I am sure we all agree that that is a very unfair and unrealistic way to run the country. If we are to establish a national petroleum company, then it is essential that the company play by the same rules as the private sector. One thing that we know for sure is that the private sector cannot obtain money for nothing. That simply does not happen. All that the amendment of the hon. member for York-Simcoe attempts to do is to suggest to the government that it must be accountable for its money, and that if it puts $1.5 billion into some project, the Canadian people should obtain some guarantee in return. If there is no guarantee in return, it is logical to request an accountability for that money. The amendment also provides that if there is some kind of return on the money, then the government should play by the same rules as the private sector.
Perhaps I could quote again the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) as recorded at page 7,205 of Hansard:
The basic response is that we think that a national petroleum corporation should be financed like every other petroleum corporation with the substantial amount of funds being put forward in risk form by way of capital, that it should be put forward in equity form rather than loan form-
I challenge the minister to tell us of any company that has such money straight from the sky. Private companies are not in the same position as the government which, in the last 40 months, printed 40 per cent more money than it had before. Private companies cannot do that. The money they have is money they earned, which has a value
July 3, 1975

attached to it, or money they borrowed. To be able to put out into the corporation $1.5 billion interest free simply means, at the rate at which money is going today, other companies are paying between 10 per cent and 12 per cent more. That gives the Crown corporation an option to operate at that much of a loss and still appear as if it were breaking even.
Let us take a look at some other Crown corporations in Canada, some to which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has chosen to refer from time to time. Let us consider some uranium companies. We know that a number of them are inefficient. For example, if we go back to 1964 we note that at that time five different companies operated in the uranium business. They were Eldorado Nuclear, Canadian Faraday, Stanrock, Denison, and Rio Algom. What happened from 1964 to 1967? All those companies showed some profit, but from that time on two companies in the private sector began to show substantial losses, perhaps because they were less efficient in their operations, and by 1971 two of the companies disappeared from the market. However, two others continued to show profit. They remained in the market manufacturing and distributing uranium. As to Eldorado Nuclear, which is a Crown corporation, it obtained $1.5 million as a gift and it also received a loan of $53 million from the federal government. As a result of different rules which the government applies to Crown corporations, we have a company which is operating inefficiently and being supported by the taxpayers of this country because it has no motive to seek to be efficient.
The amendment which is before us puts forward a minimum criterion. It puts a value on the money given to the corporation. It also suggests that the government must live up to a certain standard in financing and if it cannot do that, then it should not be competing with the private sector. If the corporation cannot compete, that means it cannot operate efficiently. The money which the government suggests should be granted to the corporation at no interest amounts to an unprecedented gift from a government to a Crown corporation. Again, I challenge the minister to tell us of any other Crown corporation which has received such money interest free. Certainly, that is not the case of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which has to pay a rate of interest on the money received, nor is it the case of the Farm Credit Corporation, which also has to pay a rate of interest on the money it receives. If the same practice were to be adopted with regard to all Crown corporations, CNR and Air Canada included, many of those companies would operate at what would appear to be a profit.
But the fact of the matter is that there would not be a profit at all because it will not be paying for the value of a dollar. If it is not paying for that, that puts it into a special status, and in part that is what is wrong with Petro-Can. If a separate status is set up and then Petro-Can is put into the same game as the private sector, that simply disrupts and makes a nervous private sector, which in the long run means that the over-all result will be a slowing down of our search for supply, rather than speeding it up, which is the basic objective upon which this bill was put forward. It cannot do otherwise, and so I think that there
Petro-Canada
are some explanations owing, and some real answers must be given by the minister. With regard to some of the responses the minister has made in committee and here in the House by saying that he has answered questions over and over again, the truth of the matter is that he has responded over and over again, but he has not given an answer because an answer has some connection with the question asked or proposes some solution which meets it.
As an example one could look at page 7205 of Hansard where the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is recorded as stating the following in response to the hon. member for York-Simcoe:
The hon. gentleman says that nobody could point out in the estimates where there was an appropriation for Petro-Canada. Madam Speaker, the bill is an appropriation for Petro-Canada; it does not appear in the estimates. That is the purpose of the bill...
On that basis the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) must provide out of cash requirements of the government for a corporation of this kind, and did provide the sum of $15 million during the current fiscal year . ..
If that was the answer, I would challenge the minister, who was asked that same question time and time again in committee, to find that answer previously anywhere in committee and to show it to us. To say to us that he had responded over and over again simply is not so, because that answer cannot be found anywhere else.

I am sure that that comment will be approved by the opposition to an even greater degree after I have finished. The reason is that all hon. members are ready and willing to see that the whole of the government projects are approved by this House before we take our adjournment. I hoped that, notwithstanding the fact that there was an agreement to debate this bill for two days, we could have shortened the debate. I was justified in that assumption in view of the interminable time which was taken by members of the opposition in 15 or 16 committee meetings to debate exactly what has been debated in the past three speeches.
The amendment which has been proposed is one which has permitted hon. members opposite to parade all the arguments they paraded before the committee, and it is indicative of the fact that they are attacking the principle of the bill. This question of capitalization is a red herring, and what they are really debating is the basic principle. They know the argument that public investment is not desirable does not wash with the Canadian public. They know that the Canadian public is no longer interested in the old Conservative regressive arguments that there ought not to be any public participation in the private sector. But they are ashamed of that argument, and they know that it does not wash with the Canadian public, so they have to find some way of hiding it. What they are doing now is to hide it under the question of capitalization by saying that $1.5 billion is too much to put into a

corporation interest free. That is an absolute fallacy, and it cannot bear any scrutiny. I invite hon. members and the Canadian public to really consider the arguments of the Tory Party.
Yesterday we had the privilege of receiving a delegation of the Swedish parliament which came to Canada. One of their comments was that they could not understand why there was so much foreign investment in Canada. They indicated that if that were the situation in Sweden, they could not live with it and that there would be a public uproar. However, Canadians have accepted that. What the Swedish delegation did not know was that in the petroleum industry, Canadians participate only to the extent of one per cent. The total Canadian participation in the oil industry is one per cent. The multinationals control 99 per cent of the petroleum industry, and that is a fact. When hon. members speak of competition, what competition is there in the private sector when the multinationals control 99 per cent of the oil industry? This government has chosen to invest in the private sector in order to enhance the position of Canadians within the industry.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) cited Eldorado as an example of a company which is not acceptable, and that proves that there has been a failure by the public sector in enterprise. I would be pleased if the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) would indicate how public investment in Eldorado has kept alive a community called Elliot Lake over a time when there was softness in the uranium market. This investment has permitted the Canadian nuclear industry, to participate to a greater extent than otherwise would have been the case. Canada now is at the forefront in the nuclear industry with the CANDU reactor as well as with the supply of uranium. At that time there was foresight in the public sector which was not available in the private sector to invest in that industry to keep it alive, and as a result of it being kept alive we now have the possibility of involving ourselves in that sector. I might point out that, although the Conservatives do not want to recognize the fact, as a result of public investment in the nuclear industry we in Canada have a control that is vested in the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on the amendment because I am dealing with the arguments which have been advanced by hon. members opposite, mainly the question of public involvement in the private sector. I am trying to indicate that, contrary to the arguments advanced by the opposition, Canada, the government and the public sector, have been successfully involved in the energy field in Canada. Eldorado is one example.
As I pointed out initially. The Tories are drawing a red herring across the path, trying to show in this instance that they do not really have any philosophical disagreement with the involvement of the public sector in the energy field. If we listen to the hon. member for Calgary

Dealing with the comments made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), you do not pay inter-
Petro-Canada
est on common shares. Common shares are not funds on loan; they are a subscription for capital in which the subscriber takes the chance that he may lose his capital investment altogether. Of course, he has the hope that over a period of time the capital will earn money and he will get a return by way of dividends.
In relation to petroleum corporations generally, very substantially the risk capital that has been put forward for exploration in particular is in the common share form or what has accrued on common shares, namely, the retained earnings of the corporation, and in that sense there is no interest paid. It is not a loan. The investor takes his chances on the success of the operation. This is with regard to the common shares.
I recommend to the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour) that he read the bill again. The bill clearly provides that the present government and governments in the future can provide an additional $1 billion dollars, as it may decide from time to time, either in loan form or preferred shares form, with no restriction on one or the other within that amount. It does provide for certain conditions under which loans may be made or preferred shares may be issued and subscribed for.
At this time I do not think I should try to tie the hands of this or any other government as to what the split would be between preferred shares and funded debt. From the standpoint of the minister in favour of a corporation engaged in the very high-risk task of exploration for petroleum, very naturally I would hope to get the funds in preferred share form, with the stipulation like that with common shares, that I would not be confined to a periodic payment by way of a fixed cumulative dividend. Really, though, this would be in the form of risk capital.
In order to get the additional funds for participation in auxiliary activities or pipeline projects that might follow from the discovery of petroleum or natural gas by this particular corporation, for example, it may be that public funds would be put forward in a loan form to the particular project, and hence would be an advance by the treasury in loan form. I say to the hon. member that I will not attempt, in this House or outside, to tie the hands of future ministers or governments in this regard. There is no way I can do so.
If a substantial balance of the funds is to go for exploration, the argument I would make is that it should go in equity form and should be in preferred shares. If it is to be by way of lending to a pipeline project as further financing in which the corporation may be interested, it would obviously not only be sensible that it should be on loan, repayable to the corporation, but the corporation in turn should raise these funds from the public treasury by way of a loan at the Crown corporation rate. This will depend on the development of the corporation, the development of its assets as time goes on.
I do not think it is of any particular value for me to give an indication now as to how the government will be lending money to the corporation for operations which at the moment have not commenced, in relation to assets which have not yet been acquired or with regard to possibilities which we hope will occur but have not yet been realized.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to discuss an important and urgent matter.
Because of the growing economic difficulties Canadian citizens are experiencing as a result of the constant rise in the cost of living, and the added negative consequences they will have to bear resulting from the last budget recently brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), especially with regard to the increase in the cost of gas and heating oil, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
July 3, 1975

subsubtopic: METHOD OF ACHIEVING IMPROVED SECURITY IN VIEW OF REDUCTION IN EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General who, following the killing of a prison guard early in the week, said "I agree something has to be done. We cannot tolerate our correctional officers being attacked like this." While he was promising the guards improved security within the prisons, did the Solicitor General explain to them how he was going to achieve this when about $11.5 million is being cut from his spending estimates with regard to additional prison staff?

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES
subsubtopic: METHOD OF ACHIEVING IMPROVED SECURITY IN VIEW OF REDUCTION IN EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some of the matters we wanted to deal with right away were a tightening of the procedures for taking prisoners on escort and for internal security within the prisons. As I pointed out last week, in the past two years we did a lot to improve perimeter security. Escapes were cut back by about 66 per cent. We would now like to make a major effort in the area of internal security and for security of escorts. The sums being cut, which were referred to by the hon. gentleman, are for the most part for new institutions, I think two. However, we are still going ahead with other maximum security institutions. They are not affected by the budget.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES
subsubtopic: METHOD OF ACHIEVING IMPROVED SECURITY IN VIEW OF REDUCTION IN EXPENDITURES
speechtext: It has been reported that the Solicitor General promised he would increase prison security and probably hire more guards. Is that a correct statement or is it correct that, as reported by the President of the Treasury Board, estimates for staff in penitentiaries will in fact be cut by some $3.6 million?

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is provision for an increase in staff for next year and the year after. I will have further discussions with the government as to whether we will increase that still further. Treasury Board and the government have already approved of increases, but there may be areas where we will have to increase still further.

speechtext:

open question, as the Solicitor General suggests? Is it correct, as the Solicitor General says, that the government cannot go ahead with the necessary new penitentiaries because communities are objecting to them, or is it correct as the President of the Treasury Board indicates that the government has cut back on the estimates for the building of new penal institutions?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE TO PROCEED WITH CONSTRUCTION OF NEW INSTITUTIONS

speechtext: My question is directed to the Solicitor General, Mr. Speaker. Does the minister think the assurance given to the guards on Sunday that he is going to give them full support, followed by the unprecedented walkout from the penitentiary system on Monday, is compatible with the statement of the President of the Treasury Board on Wednesday that dollar support is to be cut back?

I will try to make sure that whatever the cuts have been they are in areas which will not affect security.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree that each minister of the Cabinet must make a decision in his own heart whether he can support the decision of the Cabinet. When the Cabinet exercises the prerogative of mercy the ministers agree to that or they leave the Cabinet. In the contrar's case, which is hypothetical, if the Cabinet should decide on the hanging of somebody each minister would have to decide whether he could stay in the Cabinet, or whether he will support that decision.

speechtext:
1.	Is the Department of National Revenue assessing a $20,000 tariff on a 100th birthday gift to the City of Calgary made by the Dutch Canadian Centennial Committee of Calgary, of a $100,000 electronic carillon made up of 330 bells?
2.	Has the Department taken into consideration that the gift is for a charitable purpose, being Calgary's centennial year and that the carillon was not manufactured in Canada?
3.	Under what item and for what reason has the Department and the Minister assessed the $20,000 tax?
4.	Has the Department taken into consideration that other gifts made of similar class and kind to churches, etc., have been exempted from such tax?
5.	Does the Department consider that the tax must be assessed and collected and, if so, will the Minister be prepared to pass an Order in Council making the necessary refund in light of the fact that this is Calgary's centennial year and a year honouring the RCMP that held the West for Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX ON GIFT TO CITY OF CALGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer reads as follows; 1. Yes. Through its broker the Dutch Canadian Centennial Committee has requested an estimate of the duty and taxes payable in respect of a musical instrument known as a "Schumerich Americana Mark V". This instrument is electronically operated and reproduces the sounds of a carillon but does not possess bells. It has been valued at $58,194.50, and duty and sales tax payable are estimated to be $16,760.02.
2.	The tariff item under which the instrument has been imported does not permit taking into consideration the purpose of the gift or its made-in-Canada status.
3.	The duty and taxes were estimated in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Customs Tariff and the
Customs Acts. The carillon falls under tariff item 59725-1 which provides: "Musical instruments of all kinds, n.o.p." The rate of duty applicable is 15 per cent, to which is added 12 per cent sales tax.
4.	Yes. Tariff item 69605-1 permits churches and universities to import certain types of equipment not made in Canada duty free. However, in this case the gift was not made to either a church or a university.
5.	There is no statutory authority for the Department to waive assessment and collection of the duty and taxes applicable. In the past, requests that duty and taxes on gifts made under similar circumstances be remitted by way of Order in Council have been refused and it is not considered that any deviation from this policy is warranted with respect to the gift to the City of Calgary.
