subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. One must assess the purpose of the budget. The budget merely reflects the government's appraisal of economic conditions in this country and is a guideline for the government's proposed spending during the coming year.
I suggest that the budget's assessment of the economy is inadequate. In the past, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has failed to estimate correctly conditions in this country; he has not been able to say accurately how much the economy would grow in the following year. In this budget the minister said he would try to curtail government spending. Apparently the minister takes pride in saying no to his cabinet colleagues. How does he propose to cut $1 billion from government spending? Let me draw an analogy. This is like your wife, or mine, saying, "Look at all the money I saved by not buying that dress." That is how the minister proposes to save $1 billion.
He also said in his budget speech that the government will cut the federal funding of provincially-shared health programs. In other words, the minister gave notice to the provinces that they can no longer trust the federal government; it will cut down its part of the funding of federal-provincial programs. Originally, the federal government forced the provinces to enter into hospitalization agreements. The government is giving the required five-year notice. Originally, the government enticed the provinces to participate in the medicare program even though we all knew the program would be expensive. Those who spoke in the pertinent debates expressed the fear that medical health costs would grow alarmingly and that the quality of medical services would decline correspondingly. I think this has happened. Now the government has given notice of its intention to curtail its spending in this field.
In the budget, the minister suggested that medicare expenditures have increased by 20 per cent and that in the coming year the federal government will limit their growth to 13 per cent, in the following year to 12 per cent and on down until 1978, to 8.7 per cent. I suggest the minister has great confidence in being able to curtail inflation or, as is more likely the case, he is determined to shift more and more of the burden on to the backs of the provinces.
The demand for services is being placed more and more on the provincial governments and the sources of revenue left open to them are diminishing. Outside of new-found resource wealth the provincial governments have used all their sources of revenue. The demand on the federal government for services is far less than the demand on the

provincial governments. However, in this budget the federal government is moving more and more into the taxing field which is normally that of the provinces and is getting out of some of the cost-shared programs into which it in fact enticed the provinces.
I think this is a greedy budget. Some years ago there was a great deal of talk in this House about "co-operative federalism" and how it would work. Looking at this budget, it appears the Minister of Finance has long forgotten that political phrase. The budget makes a sham attempt at dealing with some of the housing problems in Canada today. The minister stated again today that there are an additional $200 million for housing. Housing starts this year are 30 per cent below those of a year ago. Certainly, more than an injection of money must be made into the housing field.
The minister commented on the unemployment situation and said he was going to divert $10 million to assist in the transfer and mobility of unemployed persons to locations within Canada where there is a shortage of labour. The minister also suggested that the Unemployment Insurance Act would be changed. At the moment it merely effects a transfer of funds from regions which have less than 4 per cent unemployment to those with more than 4 per cent unemployment: it is really a transfer of money by the labouring class through their unemployment insurance premiums. The Minister of Finance will eliminate the 4 per cent level and increase the unemployment insurance premiums. All of this is very valid. However, I remember that when the act was changed in 1971 I said the premiums would never equal the pay-out. I said the pay-out would only entice people to take unemployment insurance rather than actively seek employment or would make them a little more choosy in the employment they sought.
We look forward to the next change to the Unemployment Insurance Act to see whether the loopholes have been plugged and whether it is more an insurance program than a welfare program. When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) introduced the last Unemployment Insurance Act changes into this House, he made no bones about it; he recognized it as a social program which took into consideration the whole social aspect of unemployed workers in Canada.
The Minister of Finance said he could not reach a consensus with labour and management with regard to controlling prices, and therefore did not feel that a voluntary or compulsory program would work in controlling spiralling prices and wages. In my opinion the government has set a very poor example with regard to controlling wages and inflation. This House well remembers the spiral of inflation which started after the Pearson government granted the Seaway workers a 30 per cent wage increase. That started a round of inflation and increased wage demands. Last fall this government granted the terminal workers at Vancouver a 61 per cent pay increase. It then attempted to try to reach a consensus with regard to limiting wage increases. After setting a precedent by passing a bill in this parliament to grant one segment of society a 61 per cent increase, labourers all across Canada began to demand similar treatment. The minister has not made a concerted effort to try to reach a better under-
July 3, 1975

standing with labour regarding inflation; in fact, rather than controlling inflation, this budget has spurred it on.
As I have said, this government has moved more and more into the provincial tax field. A glaring example is the ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline. I read the speech of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). He seemed very gleeful about the fact that the provinces already tax the sale of gasoline. He stated that some provinces already have a tax of 19 cents a gallon on gasoline. That is quite understandable when one considers the origin of the tax. It is the provinces that construct the highways and roads; they impose the gasoline tax to assist the financing of bigger and better roads. The federal government are using the lame excuse that this tax will be used to firmly establish and maintain one oil price across Canada. They believe they will be in a deficit position with regard to the tax on our oil exports to the United States and that the tax will subsidize all oil purchased east of the Ottawa Valley at the international price.
If an increase of $1.50 a barrel will increase the price of gas to the consumer by five cents a gallon, it is logical to assume that a tax of ten cents a gallon would have the same effect as increasing the price of oil by $3 a barrel. The present price of oil is $8 a barrel; if it is increased by $3 it will be $11 a barrel, which is very near the international price. What is the government really doing? It is putting an additional $350 million into its coffers. The Minister of Finance said that in a full year it will amount to $450 million. It is a fact that this tax does not have to be imposed to maintain one-price oil. If we bought at the international price, we would have one price.
Whether the gasoline user knows or admits it, he is paying the same price as that charged in the international market. All one has to do is check the figures. Go to the United States and buy a gallon of gasoline. They are buying on the international market. Prices in the United States are less than they are in Canada. Of course, the gallon is smaller; it is four-fifths of the Imperial gallon. But the price works out at exactly four-fifths of what we are paying and it does not matter in what province it is bought.
Go to Vancouver. Regular gasoline is selling there at a price in the neighbourhood of 82 cents a gallon. Across the border, in the United States, you can buy gasoline-four-fifths of our gallon-at 62 cents which is four-fifths of what we are paying. East of the Ottawa Valley, motorists will be paying $1.05 a gallon for gasoline this fall. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that they could not buy it for that price if we were buying it on the international market? The tax of ten cents imposed by the Minister of Finance brings the price paid by every Canadian up to the international price in whatever province he happens to live.
It might be said we ought to be paying the international price so as to make more money available for exploration in Canada, in which case we would not, perhaps, be wondering about what would happen in five or ten years from now when we ran out of oil. I heard the Minister of Finance say on Sunday that in five or ten years our supplies would be replenished because the government was now encouraging development. That is a complete
The Budget-Mr. Horner
fabrication on the part of the minister. I say this because of the 15-cent a gallon increase in the price of gasoline brought about by the budget, less than one cent will go to exploration and the development of new oil supplies. The amount might be a little more generous in the case of natural gas because natural gas has been underpriced for so long.
It has been suggested that the changes in taxation will encourage companies to do more exploration work. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have a statement here from a finance company, Draper, Dobie and Company. This is what they say about the minister's resource taxation proposals:
In the new budget, Turner proposed to reduce the corporate tax rate for production profits from oil and gas to 46 per cent from the current 50 per cent, effective January 1, 1976. The special abatement of 15 points of federal tax is to be withdrawn at the same time. The new budget also provided an extra income deduction from income, as an allowance in recognition of provincial resource levies. The resource allowance will be prescribed by regulation to be 25 per cent of resource production profits. For purposes of this allowance, production profits will be calculated after operating expenses and capital cost allowances but before deduction of interest expense, exploration and development and earned depletion. This new resource allowance will become effective also on January 1, 1976.
It is possible that not many hon. members understand what all that means. However, the next sentence is important:
What do these two changes in taxation mean? In essence, the best way to answer that question is, nothing.
That is what a company deeply involved in trying to arrange finance for further resource development within this country thinks of the taxation proposals in the budget. They work it all out and suggest that the changes are of no significance. As one can see from the figures produced, the federal tax rate is reduced by three cents a barrel. That is what the changes in resource taxation mean as the company figures it out. They will lower the tax on oil by three cents a barrel-so the Minister of Finance has really given next to nothing.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in his contribution to the debate, addressed himself at great length to the need for higher gasoline prices. As reported on page 7100 of Hansard he had this to say:
I have argued that higher prices are necessary, firstly to bring on stream the oil and gas resources that Canadians will require in the next five to ten years; secondly, to help generate the high volume of savings necessary to find and develop these resources; and, thirdly, to reduce the rate of growth of energy demands to manageable levels.
Let us consider the first of the reasons given-to bring on stream the oil and gas resources Canadians will require in the next five or ten years. Mr. Speaker, anyone who is prepared to listen to the resource companies in Canada, whether Canadian-owned or not, can find no comfort in their words. They see nothing in the budget which will encourage them to explore for more oil. As I have just pointed out, of 15 cents a gallon increase in the price of gasoline, less than one cent goes toward the further development of our resources. The minister is not fooling anyone. Some of his own backbenchers may be fooled, but that is all.
Consider the second suggestion in the paragraph I have quoted, "to help generate the high volume of savings necessary to find and develop these resources". Mr. Speaker, I have just quoted from a paper put out by a financial

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Horner
house which is attempting to gather money to finance exploration for oil, and they say the tax proposals in the budget mean nothing. I do not doubt that their opinion is an objective one because, after all, they are trying to encourage investment in this field. The Minister of Finance told us a few months ago that Canada would need to spend $100 billion on the development of our energy resources so that we would be assured of sufficient supplies in coming decades. He said we would need to spend $100 billion by the year 2000. Be that as it may, the finance company I have quoted can find no comfort at all in this budget.
The other point the minister made in support of the budget proposals was that the new measures would reduce the rate of growth of energy demands to manageable levels. I need only remind hon. members that when the Minister of Finance was asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to tell the House how much he expected the ten cents tax would reduce gasoline consumption, the minister said he had really no idea; his department had not made an estimate. We would have to wait and see. I can answer that question right now, Mr. Speaker. It will not reduce gasoline consumption at all. It may cause some consumers to buy smaller cars, or it may encourage others to remove the anti-pollution equipment which was forced upon the car manufacturers by the government, in an effort to get better mileage. But as to the consumer staying home, not driving as much, or walking to work, I suggest the effect will be minimal. There may be a few more bicycles sold, partly because of increasing traffic congestion and partly because of a desire for exercise, but I do not believe it will be the result of the ten-cent tax.
What should the minister have done? It is obvious there is high unemployment in some areas of Canada and a need for workers in other areas. Last weekend a neighbour of mine, along with two boys, one 19 and the other 17, drove up to an oil well which was being drilled. They got out of the truck and the foreman of the drilling rig approached them and asked, "Do you boys want a job? If so, you can go to work right away because we are operating this rig with only half a crew." The boys asked what the pay would be and the foreman said it was between $5 and $6 an hour. The younger of the boys told his father that he had been offered a job right away at $5 an hour. I imagine that his father, a farmer, was not particularly pleased on that occasion, but I can add that the boy's love for agriculture was such that he did not take up the offer.
This story would indicate that some areas of Canada are actively seeking labour, while others have a surplus of people who are unemployed. To my way of thinking, the government has to make a greater effort in readjusting the list of projects on which the minister says the government is going to spend money. The minister said the government was going to spend only $10 million on the transfer of the labour force within Canada. I think that amount could have been stepped up and some of the other expenditures could have been curtailed. We have a country with a number of very definite cold spots-I refer to the lumber industry and the mining and resource industry as examples-and the minister could have made some tax conces-

sions in respect of both these industries to encourage greater expansion and exploration.
Canada today does not have the basic equipment necessary to carry on the required amount of drilling or exploration for oil and gas because much of that equipment has been moved elsewhere. We have not even encouraged the exploration companies to stay at home.
The minister has made no real effort to curtail the growth in the money supply. He might have done what is being attempted in the United States. I know that my socialist friends do not believe this is the way to curtail inflation, but it may help. In the United States, the federal reserve system is presently seeking a moderate rate of expansion in the monetary and credit aggregates. Mr. Burns said:
We believe that the course we are pursuing will promote an increase ... of between 5 per cent and 7!d per cent over the 12 months-
He was speaking of the next 12-month period. This government has printed money at an alarming rate. There are three things in relation to money that can control inflation to some extent. The first is, of course, the amount of money, the second is the speed at which it circulates, and the third is the amount of credit given out which is based upon the money supply at any given time.
It is interesting to note that in answer to a question I put to the Minister of Finance, he said that in the U.S. there has been a curtailment of consumer credit by consumers generally. He said, in a letter he wrote me on June 6, that recent levels are down to $152.3 billion in credit outstanding in the United States. He went on to suggest that in Canada there is no appropriate figure, but on the basis of the figures of 80 per cent of the companies, one could estimate that outstanding consumer credit is continuing to grow; in the first quarter of 1975 it reached a figure of better than $16 billion, and at the end of March it was $16.6 billion. If one makes a rough comparison between Canada and the United States, using the 10 per cent formula, he will readily see that proportionately Canadians have a larger balance of consumer credit outstanding at this time.
The minister, in my opinion, should have brought in some measures of control credit. This might have slowed the circulation of money within Canada and perhaps would have had a beneficial effect on inflation. In my opinion, this would have done less harm to the consumer, and it would be the easiest thing to remove at any time in the future when the country needed some impetus in the form of additional expenditure.
Let me say a word or two about the gasoline tax. I understand that about 50 per cent of a barrel of oil goes to the production of gasoline, so really the tax only applies to 50 per cent of each barrel of oil produced. In the transportation study this government has just produced, it is stated that only 13 per cent of the energy consumed by Canadians today is used in the form of gasoline. If we are going to curtail energy used by a ten-cent tax per gallon of gasoline, we will only curtail 13 per cent of all energy used. That is a very weak argument put forward by the Minister of Finance.
There is growing concern and apprehension on the part of Canadians all across the country about what is going to
July 3, 1975

happen next. Normally, the budget reassures the people that everything is in the hands of the Minister of Finance, who has a firm grip on things. One of the interesting revelations in this budget is that the Minister of Finance does not have a firm grip on things. We have all seen in many daily newspapers, in eastern Canada particularly and perhaps all across the country, the suggestion that this government can no longer control government expenditure. That is the thought that has been conveyed by this budget and it does not allay the growing fears and apprehensions of Canadians who feel that the country has run amok and we are headed for big trouble. I think the Minister of Finance could have reassured the people to a greater extent than he did.
Even the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), in his speech during the budget debate, suggested that 70 per cent of government spending is already ordained to be spent in such a manner that the government cannot intercede to curtail it. The government should have brought in a measure to curtail credit. It should also have provided the impetus to encourage further resource development in the mining and oil and gas industries.
The government should have brought forward measures to assist house construction to a greater degree. It should also have provided some encouragement to the lumber industry. These are industries where there is a great deal of employment and by encouraging them the government might have taken care of many of the unemployed in this country. The government should also have brought forward a provision extending its participation in the movement of the labour force from high unemployment areas to areas where there is a need for manpower.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raynald Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General I would like to begin my comments this afternoon, in reply to the budget speech tabled last week, by a brief history of the current conflict in the Post Office.
The labour contract passed between the Post Office on the one hand and the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada and the Union of Postal Workers on the other hand expired on December 31, 1974. Before the expiration of the contract the Council of Postal Unions, which had represented the Letter Carriers' Union and the Union of Postal Workers since the coming into force of the 1967 Public Service Labour Relations Act, was disbanded by the Public Service Labour Relations Board with the consent of both unions involved.
The Letter Carriers' Union and the Union of Postal Workers were recognized as bargaining agents in the month of January 1975. Negotiations ended in February and the settlement of the conflict was entrusted to a conciliation board presided by Lome Clarke. An agreement in principle between both parties was reached on April 24 last. The new agreement covering 30 months provided an over-all increase of 38 per cent-an average salary of $12,771 for letter carriers. After eight meetings the Union of Postal Workers could not reach an agree-
The Budget-Mr. R. Guay
ment, and on June 19 last Mr. Justice Rene Lippe was appointed conciliator and commissioned to produce a report on the conflict.
The Post Office pursued two objectives and is still pursuing those two objectives-reaching a fair and equitable collective agreement as well as improving the service so it will become the best in the world. The Post Office must fulfill its responsibility which is to offer to the people of this country a modern and efficient service. However, if the Post Office has responsibilities, so does the postal employee, and one of the most important is to understand fully the need for automation and accept it as indispensable and unavoidable. Without automation employees would disappear more rapidly than with automation. We state once again, as parliamentary secretary- and I repeat, as the minister stated previously-that not one employee of the Post Office will lose his job because of automation.
There is another matter, Mr. Speaker, which worries me at the present time and it is the problem of jobs for students. With the summer months, our students have arrived on the labour market. This is the best opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to consider a few moments the situation of students, that is our children, as a result of available employment and consequently to speak about the Opportunities for Youth Program. When the well-intentioned government created that program, it wanted to help students by making available paid jobs requiring creativity and a sense of responsibilities. However, due to its lack of impact on our young people, I will not beat around the bush and suggest the unconditional abolition of the Opportunities for Youth Program, as I had the chance to mention it privately and publicly. We want to help the young people and the government is aware of that. We could do it in many ways and here are a few suggestions. The LIP program, which was created to encourage employment but which does not achieve that aim because it does not ensure the permanence of projects it launches, could be changed so that the more interesting projects be approved and kept alive for periods of one two or three years as necessary, but long enough to allow the continuation of projects on a permanent basis after the withdrawal of grants.
The LIP projects could be organized so as to provide jobs for a number of students in summer. Grants could be made available for this purpose, which on the one hand would have the advantage of bringing new manpower to projects already under way and, on the other hand, of enabling students to hobnob with people from another world than their own. The students would also benefit from the experience gained by the other participants in the projects. Speaking of the LIP program, let me refer now to my letter dated June 21, 1975 to the minister in which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) announced a further program for 1975. Considering the difficulties now faced by municipalities-specially in Quebec-in covering their expenditures, I believe that this year LIP projects be accepted on the basis mainly that they be community projects of municipal nature.
So it is now realized that our young people have no interest in business or economic activities in general. I feel, however, that if businesses, industries, manufacturers,

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. R. Guay
shops received the full amount of salaries to be paid to student help, a good number of jobs would be created and young people would get useful experience, which would ensure an ample supply of future applicants.
I would now turn to the New Horizons Program. This program also could be changed to provide summer employment for students willing to care for the aged. Lonely elder people would welcome the opportunity to spend a few months of every year among our youth.
There is no doubt, on the other hand, that young people would benefit tremendously from human contact with their elders. The main problem faced by young people looking for their first jobs is that everywhere they will be asked one, two or three years' experience. But there is no way they could have gained such experience because our present summer employment system gives no training whatsoever for the trade they will be plying. So, less emphasis should be put on inventing programs and more on being practical. Let us all work together to devise ways to find jobs for our young people in their future fields of endeavour and I am sure they will thank us for it later.
Another issue which is of great concern to me and all hon. members of the House is one which was criticized at length by all information media as well as opposition members. Personally, not only do I want to criticize the oil issue, but I should like also to make a number of propositions which seem to me to be quite logical. As I was saying, the last issue which I want to deal with and which is the main feature of this budget, at least as far as the interest it has generated is concerned, is that of energy. Although we all knew that an increase in oil prices was forthcoming, the decisions taken about our energy policy for the current year took everybody by surprise, including I think the members of the ruling party. Faced with a serious dilemma, the Minister of Finance must assure both long and short term production of oil, in order that the consuming public may not have to suffer from the lack of foresight in this area. Of course, achieving that objective will be no easy matter but some of the means to be resorted to in doing so were announced in the budget. The effort is praiseworthy, but I do deplore the fact that in spite of some of the exemptions provided to lighten the burden inflicted upon the consumers, obviously, the low wage-earner will suffer the most from increased prices, that is, the one who has no business, who cannot deduct his travelling expenses, the one who must drive his car to work, the small wage-earner, who has only 15 days off a year and who, now will be unable to spend them visiting his country, as television commercials entice him to do, that activity now having become a luxury.
The second point I found surprising was the incentives the federal government deemed advisable to provide for the oil companies to bring them to invest adequate amounts in prospecting.
Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that since the companies make millions of dollars of profits by taking from our country a non-renewable natural resource, the government would have been entitled to demand that these companies reinvest a certain percentage of their benefits in the exploration for new oil fields. This would have 
pleased me, and I am certain that I am not the only one to think this, because it is quite natural. Mr. Speaker, since we are anxious about future production and reserves, I believe that now would be the time to think very seriously about developing new energy forms, such as nuclear energy, and to invest in this area if possible.
At the last conference of provincial premiers, the premier of New Brunswick insisted on this issue. Unfortunately, its seems that the voice of the western premiers was heard better than his own, since the government shows some reluctance when it should go forward and maybe innovate more. They are afraid of the unknown, of this possible solution. How can they not be fearful of all kinds of disasters: ecological, economic, financial and political brought about by traditional formulas, since these are very evident.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to note that I wanted to be very positive and that I would not like hon. members, even in this part of the House, to think that I simply wanted to criticize. My comments on the issue of energy are not a destructive criticism like those I heard during the five days of the debate. I am still waiting for opposition members to suggest practical solutions. When I have the opportunity to speak in the House, I always wait for the official opposition to really play its role, not simply to criticize, but also to make suggestions.
All this week again, Mr. Speaker, journalists did the same thing as the opposition.
I have here a copy of the budget speech. The only thing people remember about it, Mr. Speaker, is the energy problem. Surely there is more to a budget than that. Some reporters ask me: "What do you think, Mr. Guay, about what is going on with regard to energy and price increases?" I reply: "If prices are increased as a means of assurance or precaution .. . indeed, we have not been elected for a one-year period only, we must not only adopt measures for one, two or three years. We have to draw up an energy policy for the next 50 or 60 years.
Needless to say, a person of 70 doesn't care about the future. But if a person really wants to govern our country and if a minister does as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) did and assumed his responsibilities when he brought down his budget in the House, all will be well. I don't pretend to have a printing press. No member of this House can claim that we can print as much money as we want. We must actually raise money through means which, in our opinion, are the most reasonable and cause the least harm, and I deplored that fact earlier. I am not the only one to feel the pinch of inflation when I fill up my gas tank.
Of course, we could have refrained from raising oil prices, saying: That is all right, we will consume what we have. We still have reserves for ten more years. We will not do any exploration, we will not do any prospection. We will not make any investment to discover new energy sources. That would have been very simple. Mr. Speaker, that would have been the easiest and the most profitable thing to do on the political level, but the Minister of Finance has shown that he had been elected and called into the Cabinet to see ahead, to govern and run this country in the better interest of the people and not only, as I was saying earlier, for two or three years, but to build
July 3, 1975

a country which could really rank among the best in the present world.
Mr. Speaker, very often I take pleasure in attacking newspapermen. As I said the other day, when intervening in a debate when we discussed the estimates of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, we are scaring businessmen and industrialists. We are told-as I was saying the other day to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees)-that everything goes wrong here, that everything is wrong in this country. There is nothing we can do about industries and nothing we can do to help. Well, I say that is absolutely untrue. What does the average businessman in the small communities of our ridings, whether he is a shopkeeper, a manufacturer or something else, think when he hears or reads reports in the papers that everything is in a mess? So he won't even inquire with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, he will not even try to obtain information from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, he just listens to people in the opposition. In the past two or three years, Mr. Speaker, we have heard nothing but criticism about the unemployment insurance program. I myself took part in the debate on the new bill. We realized that a number of things had to be changed, and in this budget we are introducing changes.
Mr. Speaker, no one in Canada, except those who went and got a copy of the budget speech from Information Canada, knows that at least seven amendments have been proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it more flexible and more responsive to the needs of today's unemployed workers.
Mr. Speaker, I may criticize as a member of parliament, but I believe the duty of any member of parliament in the House of Commons, not only on the government side but also on the opposition side, is to express criticism on behalf of his constituents and of Canadians as a whole. He has to be an information agent.
The public in general know little about the budget. We have heard only about energy. But there are other matters involved. Take housing for instance. No one talks about it. Let us take the one billion dollar cut in government spendings which are to be reinvested in other sectors with a more urgent need for that money. Let us think of LIP programs. I was talking about young people earlier. Funds have been provided, they will increase. We will change some projects for public housing, moderately priced rental housing and other things. That is something the public are unaware of, and it is quite unfortunate. I am definitely not saying that I am the only member of parliament willing to inform the Canadian people.
But I find that there are not enough hon. members, especially on the opposition side, who are playing the part for which they were elected. Their job is not to try to destroy a political party, be it Liberal, New Democratic, Social Credit or Progressive Conservative, but to come here and set up policies for the welfare of every Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, when we look on what is going on in society, we wonder if it is not a little-and I think that today more than ever we must reflect upon that-if all the unrest in our society is not due to a lack of information, if it is not precisely due to the politicians who are not playing the part they should within society.
The Budget-Mr. R. Guay
I may go far in my assertions but I think, Mr. Speaker, that if we wish to play our part-and I approve what the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and several other members said the other day-it is important to talk about the business of the House. To be able to give information, we must have the time to go in our ridings and meet our constituents. On behalf of several members on this side I wish to say out loud what others are thinking.
If we consider that we began this session more than 10 months ago we are almost in mid-July and we are still here. If we also consider what happened during the present session, we had debates for several weeks here in this House or in committees on issues that I did not consider essential. Then at the end of the session we are faced with bills that we are supposed to pass in a hurry. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a suggestion and I think that it will be accepted by several members: first we should establish a fixed date system for the session as was suggested several times. In fact, I know that on this side, on the government side, we are working on several things and I would like to propose a set day for the Speech from the Throne and the adjournment.
But at the time of the Speech from the Throne, the government with the leaders of the House and the leaders of all parties should immediately table all the bills to be discussed during the session. If there are 50 there will be 50 and if there are 60 there will be 60. And immediately, the government leader with the leaders of the other opposition parties should agree to set our priorities and limit the debates on each bill. So, at the beginning of the session there will be less pressure, members will be more rested, calmer and debates will be limited. If there is a bill on energy it is all right. We shall take 15 or 20 days but not 40 or 60 just to have to rush a bill of this importance.
That is what I suggest, Mr. Speaker. We could go back to our ridings, we could also be on holidays during July, just as many Canadians in construction and in shipbuilding are now on holidays just as our children are also on holidays. And there are ever more young Parliament members on this side as well as on the opposite side of the House. We have young children who do not see their father. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, when I look at the situation-I wonder if I will make a joke that will be well taken-my own children now call me "Uncle" because I cannot be at home very often. But I believe that we must have contact not only with our family, which is quite normal, but also with our own constituents.
When I suggested a moment ago that we should inform our constituents, that would give us much more time to visit our ridings, to inform people in a very calm and relaxed way. We could say to our people: There are some facts. We are coming to meet you, to discuss with you certain bills and some of our plans. We are looking forward to a Speech from the Throne in September. During summer, we could travel around our ridings to meet local officials, chambers of commerce and other social organizations. We could be in a better position to make suggestions to the government which has to prepare the Speech from the Throne as well as a 12- or 15-month session. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we could be much more effective, we could

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. R. Guay
represent our constituents in a much more effective and responsible manner.
Before closing my remarks, I want to talk about a highly controversial matter if the questions asked this afternoon are a yardstick. As I have always said and preached in this House, I have spoken on a number of occasions about capital pubishment, a subject that is always discussed in a highly emotional manner. I think the issue of capital punishment has really been shifted.
Instead of talking about the reasons that have led a murderer to commit a crime, we discuss mostly the future of the murderer. We really should consider the causes for committing a murder. What should be reformed in the judiciary field? Abolitionists often say: Those who are in favour of capital punishment are very often the same who favour abortion. I shall get back to that question later. Those who are in favour of capital punishment often expose themselves to hanging innocent people. Of course, Mr. Speaker, miscarriage of justice has happened before, but what should be changed in that case: the sentence? Or else, is it that our legal system does not allow for adequate evidence? Is it not the full burden of proof, the issue of doubt, is it not all that we have to weigh when we debate capital punishment?
I have always said and I still maintain, Mr. Speaker, that I shall always be in favour of capital punishment. I will always oppose the abolition of the death sentence. It is not the question of sentence we have to discuss in this House. I hope that the debate will take place in early fall, when we want to amend the act, and I will be one of those taking part in the debate. We shall have to talk not about the sentence to be meted out to the murderer, but the whole judiciary reform, the penitentiary reform, the reform of the Criminal Code, particularly as I said earlier, the burden of proof, the issues of doubt and bail.
This afternoon, a bill has been tabled by a member on the other side on the question of carrying firearms. We had been promised all those things when the bill was initially introduced in 1967, and I will have the opportunity to analyze all that when the debate takes place. I wonder how far we have gone from 1967 until now, since capital punishment has been abolished, which improvement we have made in judiciary reform, in penitentiary reform, in the rehabilitation of delinquents and of youth. Did we achieve anything in that field? This is the question I am putting to myself. I do not give any answer now.
Others very often speak of abortion. Recently we had the opportunity to table something in the House. It may be the last subject I will touch on this afternoon, I mean the question of abortion. Abolitionists say: How funny! Most of the people advocating capital punishment are against abortion. I am one of those! Yes indeed, I am in favour of the death sentence and against abortion, because we are justly told: "You want to hang a man, you want to hang a woman, you want to hang somebody who has committed a murder, but you do not want to let innocents be born, people who did not ask to come on earth. Of course, Mr. Speaker! But the only thing I wish, as a member of parliament, would be to take part in a discussion with 4,000 or
5,000	people, as I did recently on Parliament Hill. These thousands of people gathered here to ask that the abortion legislation be amended in order to have the word "health"

defined much more clearly, much more precisely because we have given an overly wide meaning to the word. We will have to amend the Criminal Code.
I had the opportunity to discuss this on several occasions with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) when I was his parliamentary secretary, and it seems to me it would be very simple and that all parties in this House could agree to hold a very short debate on abortion, to amend the act so that it is better understood and particularly better applied. As a matter of fact, the act is not permissive; it does not allow abortion; the act defines and must define the cases and the circumstances in which abortion could be performed. This is simply what the act says and I shall have later the opportunity to be much more explicit, when both question on which I am considerably concerned come back, this fall I hope, or at least as soon as possible. I have tried to be as positive as possible in this short speech, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the characteristic comment prior to the introduction of the abortive budget of June 23 was that the Canadian economy was probably in the worst shape of any period since the depression, and since the budget came down there has been very little reason to change one's view about that. Not only is unemployment very high, but it is rising, and domestically-generated inflation is not falling as rapidly as inflation in many other countries, particularly in countries with which we trade. Export sales are down, and because of high domestic costs, imports are replacing many Canadian goods on our domestic market.
The net result is we have the most serious deficit in our balance of payments that we have had in recent history. As a consequence, the dollar is floating down and although the government has been protecting it somewhat by the use of the foreign exchange equalization account, the value of the Canadian dollar against the American dollar is declining. The price of our imports is rising, contributing to our inflation, and devaluation is not increasing our exports. On the contrary, devaluation is simply leading to higher costs, which in turn will mean fewer exports, as Great Britain found out to her horror.
So this was the sad picture of the Canadian economy on June 23, 1975, and against this sad picture all the advice the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) seemed to get was that he should not do anything at all-and that is apparently the advice he followed. Has there ever been a greater indictment of any Minister of Finance in Canadian history than the present budget? At a time when we are experiencing some of the most serious economic problems we have had, there is a complete failure of intellectual and moral leadership by the government.
The Minister of Finance, clearly, could not decide what the major problems of the economy are-whether they are unemployment, inflation and/or energy. In a traditional, old-fashioned, often discredited approach he tried to deal with all three, and with all three he failed. When dealing with unemployment, he revived the LIP program and some other make-work projects of that sort. They will not effectively deal with the unemployment issue in this coun-
July 3, 1975

try which so far is centred in the construction industry, some resource industries and some of our export manufacturing firms. Moreover, the minister did not deal with any reform whatsoever in the unemployment insurance program other than to shift the cost to the private sector.
To immediately work on the unemployment problem in this country, what he should have done was deal with the problem of housing. Housing starts are down, in 1975, to 175,000. On a per capita basis, this is the lowest level of housing construction since 1946. In this country we need
210,000	housing units per year just to stay even with the rate of new family formations.
Why is housing doing so badly? It is, as I pointed out before, because the government has not recognized that the policy it is using to deal with housing simply will not work. Housing in Canada since the end of World War II has always been counter-cyclical in the sense that when the economy was declining interest rates were falling and housing starts began to increase. But now, as the Minister of Finance has failed to recognize that we are not operating in the traditional trade-off position that we had for so many years after the end of the war, we do not have a decline in the rate of inflation as unemployment rises, we do not have a decline of interest rates and, as a consequence, there has been no increase in the amount of housing constructed in the country. The minister still believes the statement that higher interest rates are one of the most effective anti-inflationary policies that we can follow, in spite of all the evidence to the contrary, that the greatest rates of inflation we have had in Canada have been during periods of the highest interest rates.
If the government had any real intention of dealing with housing for social, humane or even economic reasons, it would have introduced a program to subsidize interest rates, as suggested by this opposition party, on mortgages in order to get the amount of housing construction increased and to help solve the unemployment situation. But because the government is limited in its thinking about economic policy to two things that it has done in the past, nothing was done to increase housing.
What about inflation, Mr. Speaker? The strongest antiinflation policy that could have been used in this country would have been to do something about housing. There is no doubt that one of the most inflationary forces that we have in the economy at the present time is the rapid increase in rents and the rapid increase in housing prices. Clearly, if the minister wanted to cope with inflation he would have done something to increase the supply of housing so that rents and housing prices could be brought down.
One of the first things to happen when rents go up is that the person who has to pay the rent seeks a higher wage-and higher wages mean higher costs, and higher costs mean higher prices. By not dealing with the housing problem at all in this budget, we are not dealing with unemployment and we are not dealing with inflation.
What about the consensus program that the minister talked about for so long? After going around the country for months insisting to the people of Canada that the economy was in a healthy state, that nothing needed to be done, that all our problems were coming from abroad, the minister now has the temerity to say in his budget that the
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
people of Canada are not willing to accept any sort of tough proposals to deal with inflation and are not willing to accept any sort of voluntary guidelines.
How astonishing that the minister would find it unusual that the people of Canada would not accept some sort of restraint after he had told them for a year or a year and a half that it was totally unnecessary! One could use an old biblical expression; I am not quite clear where it came from, but over 2,000 years ago the jawbone of an ass was used as a weapon. Now we seem to have the same thing happening in Canada, with just about the same effect. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance misled the Canadian people about the problems of the Canadian economy. Then, when the situation became critical, he was astonished that the people would not support any sort of program to try to do something about the difficulties.
What does the Minister of Finance say about inflation? Absolutely nothing. He is still misleading the Canadian people that it will probably go away. He says he is cutting expenditures by $1 billion. Of course, he is not. The fact is that expenditures are going up over 12 per cent. To suggest that by talking down his colleagues from their original demands for increased expenditures he is in fact doing something about expenditures is totally misleading. As I suggested, expenditures are going up by 12 per cent and are not going down at all.
Because of his inability to deal with expenditures or to forecast revenues, the deficit is going up by $600 million, to $3.6 billion-a fantastic inflationary force in the economy at the present time. The minister says he is going to get the money to finance this deficit from the capital markets. His cash needs are going from $114 billion to $5 billion, and he thinks he can finance this without a substantial change in interest rates. The fact of the matter is, with these cash requirements because of the huge deficit which the minister has been unable to control, we are going to find that interest rates will be forced up even higher and we will have more inflation. What has become abundantly clear in this country is that our interest rates are inflationary. This budget, that was to deal with unemployment, with inflation and with energy, has had the opposite effect in terms of inflation to what the minister thought it would have. It is a highly inflationary budget- one of the most inflationary budgets to be brought down in Canada in recent times.
Any time the deficit goes from $600 million to $3.6 billion and the cash requirements go from $114 billion to $5 billion it cannot be argued by anyone that it is not an inflationary budget. It will have an inflationary force on the Canadian economy. Most importantly, the effect of the increases brought in by the minister will be on prices and not on production, so the net result will be highly inflationary, without doing anything about the unemployment situation prevailing in the economy at the present time.
The budget has failed to deal with unemployment or with inflation. As an anti-inflationary policy, it has failed. What about energy? As was expected, the price of crude oil at the wellhead was raised by $1.50, to $8 a barrel. No one quarrelled very much with that. Some adjustments were expected, and some adjustments were made in the tax levies to try to bring increased stimulation to explora-

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
tion. What was totally unexpected in the budget, however, was the excise tax of ten cents per gallon on gasoline-the most regressive form of taxation that the government could have contemplated. It is a tax that bears equally hard on the poor and the rich, a tax that is regressive in every sense.
Why the government would bring in a ten-cent excise tax at this time is beyond comprehension. It is highly inflationary; it will add 1 Vi points to the consumer price index, and it will be an administrative nightmare to try to recover the rebates which the government has promised to provide to people at the end of the year. Most importantly, it goes to a principle that we have never followed in this country, namely, that when we have a national policy, in this case of equalization of oil prices across the country, this national policy should be paid for by some sort of consumer-user cost.
One cannot conceive of any more ineffective, regressive form of taxation than the excise tax, which again demonstrates that the Minister of Finance really does not care about the inflationary situation. This form of taxation, this direct taxation, is the most inflationary type that could have been put on at the present time. It does nothing to contribute to the discovery and development of oil in Canada. It does nothing but add revenue to the coffers of the federal government.
It has been argued by the government that they need this ten-cent tax because of the equalization program. I would ask, as has the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), if it would not be possible to find the money necessary to keep the equalization program going by cutting expenditures. In the $30 billion budget, all that the Minister of Finance had to find to support the equalization program was about a l'A per cent cut in expenditures. He did not do this; he put on an excise tax which is inflationary, difficult to operate and which goes against all sorts of principles in terms of the way in which our country should be financed.
When the Minister of Finance brought down the budget he said he wants do to three things; solve unemployment, reduce inflation, and deal with the question of energy. Any thinking person must conclude that he has failed. Not one of his policies will strengthen Canada's economy effectively, as he hoped. The fascinating question is this: Why should there be such a failure? Why should Canada, a resource-rich country, find it so difficult to provide reasonably full employment for its people, find it so difficult to maintain relative price stability, and find it so hard to operate its economy at close to its full potential? Why are we in this mess? Why have things gone so wrong?
I reject out of hand the minister's defence that we are in our present position because these problems are worldwide. Of course there are worldwide economic problems. Of course there are terribly serious international problems to be faced. That does not mean we cannot do something to solve the problems in our own country. Indeed, it is a generalization to say that economic problems are of a worldwide nature, for such generalizations do not take into account differences between various economies.

The United States and Japan, for example, for a while experienced a higher rate of inflation than ours because they had to pay for oil imported from abroad and we did not. West Germany's performance in terms of unemployment, inflation and balance of payments has been substantially superior over the years to Canada's performance. The British performance has been substantially worse, but that country operates under a planned economy.
It is senseless arguing whether or not this economy or that economy has performed better or worse than our own economy. The point is that for the last few years the Canadian economy has not been operating at its potential. It ought to have performed better than it has. I think any independent observer would concede that in the last three or four years the performance of the Canadian economy, in terms of unemployment and inflation, has been poorer than at any time since the end of World War II.
What are we to do about this? Can anything be done about it? I think everyone recognizes our poor performance, but no one seems willing to act. It must be recognized that economic conditions have changed immensely, that conditions under which the economy operated between 1946 and the 1960s no longer exist. But we are still making economic policy on the basis of past assumptions. We still assume that when there is a rise in unemployment we shall see a drop in inflation rates, or that to slow down the rate of inflation we must slow down the economy and accept unemployment. These ideas are as outmoded in Canada as they are in other countries, and the analysis which flows from these ideas is incorrect. Economic ideas and tools which were used after the end of World War II are no longer appropriate for today's economy.
Why do I say this? Forecasts of economic performance in Canada have been ludicrously wrong for the last three or four years. The forecasts for revenue for this year are incorrect by over $2 billion. Estimates of the rate of unemployment and inflation have been wrong for the last two or three years. Why? The reason is that they are based on an analysis of the economy which is not correct. We need a totally new approach to economic policy-making in Canada. As a nation, we cannot afford to lurch from excessive expansion to excessive contraction; we cannot afford deficit after deficit and error after error. We need to take economic policy-making in Canada out of the back room and debate it effectively, because now there is less debate on economic policy-making in Canada than there is in any other western industrialized democracy.
I have never heard of any other minister of finance bringing down a budget which does not estimate the country's economic rate of growth for the coming year, which does not estimate rates of unemployment or which does not project inflation rates. Only in Canada does the Minister of Finance bring down a budget which does not contain these fundamental facts, facts which need to be considered and debated in an orderly way.
When economic policy is made in Canada, the advice of outsiders is looked on as the advice of intruders. The government does not look on outsiders as people who try to help it formulate an effective economic policy. The involvement of outsiders in economic policy-making in Canada is discouraged, not encouraged. This, definitely, must change because no matter what is said, our economic
July 3, 1975

policies have not worked in the last three or four years, and since they have not worked, obviously we should examine the circumstances in which economic policies are made. We should be asking all people to put their ideas forward as to how our economy should be operated. We should be opening the doors, so to speak, and encouraging the inflow of fresh ideas as quickly as possible. This is important for Canada. Economic policy-making is far too important to be left to politicians, who feel they are doing a fine job if they survive politically. Surely the situation has gone beyond that point.
I hope hon. members will support my private member's bill which, if passed, will require the governor of the Bank of Canada to appear before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs every six months to outline the monetary policies which the bank proposes to follow. The purpose of the bill is not in any sense to limit the authority, power or responsibility of the governor of the Bank of Canada. Its purpose is to bring into the open discussion and debate on how monetary policy in this country is formulated. The bill would require the governor to tell the committee what the economic and monetary policy thrust of the bank will be. It would require him to come before the committee six months later and explain any possible deviation from that policy. The measure would allow us to discuss in the open the manner in which monetary policy is made in this country.
Such a discussion is important for Canada, as the money supply of this country has grown more quickly than the money supply of any other country in the western world, with the possible exception of Great Britain. That growth, of course, is one of the major reasons for our rate of inflation. But my main reason for introducing this bill is that it would bring economic policy-making into the public arena where it ought to be. When I suggest economic policy-making is not carried out in the public arena, I am not criticizing the governor of the Bank of Canada. This is how things are done under our system; but our system is not working. We need to debate; we need to discuss; we need to provide input. Our policy-making in this field must be in the public arena.
I also think it absolutely essential that the report of the Economic Council of Canada should be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. The committee should be given the outlook for the economy. The minister and his associates should be prepared to discuss the report of the council of economic advisers and say with what parts they agree and with what parts they disagree. In West Germany, the country with the best economic performance in the western world, that is precisely what the minister of finance must do. An economic report is tabled or presented. The minister must respond to it. He must show why it is wrong, if it is, and why his policies are better. The debate is in public-and that country's performance speaks for itself.
People outside the government need to provide far greater input into economic policy-making in Canada than is the case at present. We must use all the ideas we can, and the government must respond. Our policy-makers must be given the chance in public to justify what they are doing. After all, the world is changing, economies have changed, and the Canadian economy has changed
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
immensely. Policies which were appropriate in the 1950s and the 1960s are not working in the 1970s and it is very unlikely that they will work in future. We must find solutions.
The message of the June 23 budget is clear. We must have a basic re-examination of policy-making in this country. If we can have a budget such as the one brought down on June 23 in the face of the difficulties we have in our economy, clearly something is wrong. There are no immediate or magic solutions to the problems of inflation, unemployment, potential growth fulfilment, balance of payments, high interest rates, and so on. No one suggests there are. What I am suggesting is while there are no immediate, easy or new solutions, the old solutions are not credible either. As long as we insist on applying the old solutions to the new problems we will have difficulties such as we have at the present time.
In the forties, after World War II, country after country decided that no longer could the people of their nations stand the ravages of the business cycle such as occurred in western industrialized democracies for over a century. They decided to make it the responsibility of the government to provide a framework, through their economic policies, for ensuring full employment with reasonably stable prices. The science of economics, if it can be called a science, developed sufficiently that they were able to follow such policies for the period 1945 to 1965, and in that period there were no serious depressions such as ravaged the world before 1945. We have now entered a stage where the policies which worked effectively at that time will work no longer.
I would argue that the adoption in 1945 of policies that provided full employment and reasonable price stability was one of the principal reasons for social democracies, such as we know them, surviving. If we had gone through a serious depression in the 1950s like the one of the thirties, the sort of democracy we now know would not be in existence today.
We must find a way of dealing with the new economic situation that we face. It is just as critical as that of the thirties in the sense that we are getting shorter cycles, greater dimensions of inflation and higher unemployment all coming closer together. Unless we find a way of dealing with these problems, it will be difficult for our democracies to survive.
The great post-war period is over, the period when we had such a high level of sound economic performance. Economic structures are different both nationally and internationally. New approaches are necessary. Surely that must be the lesson of the budget of June 23. The old methods of dealing with problems such as unemployment and inflation simply do not work. We must change. As far as Canada is concerned, the first step must be to open up the whole area of policy-making. There must be debate and policy-making in totally new dimensions. While the budget of June 23, by any conventional standard, must be considered an absolute disaster, to the extent that it focused attention on the fact that we need reform in our economic policy making, and soon, because our problems
7246

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
continue at such great magnitude, it may in fact have served some purpose.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure Canadians will derive great comfort from the message just delivered by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and the alternative he has put forward for our consideration. This will become more clear when we have had an opportunity to read his speech and draw our own conclusions.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for producing a budget under such uncertain and difficult economic conditions, steering a path between worldwide inflation and recession. I am grateful to the government for having resisted the temptation to adopt wage and price controls. Such a measure would allow too many loopholes and exemptions; it would allow the stronger elements in our society, such as the professionals, to find means of avoiding controls and retain their competitive position, while the weaker elements would remain where they are and continue to be weak.
It is a measure that would be effective with wage and salary earners but not with persons earning other types of income. It would not affect the farmers; nor would it affect the price of imports. It would be an unfair measure because it would apply effectively to wage and salary earners but not to others. It is for this reason that we, as Liberals, reject the notion of controls and believe in the approach of self-imposed restraints as the only sensible measure in a political democracy.
The Liberal government's approach to inflation has been one of encouraging production in order to increase supply, removing tariffs, reducing federal taxes, increasing pensions and family allowances, and making income tax deductions. This government introduced the concept of rolling back excessive profits in the budget of May last year. That measure protects the consumer from price gouging. It is badly needed and we hope it will be incorporated into legislation in the not too distant future.
In the past few days I have been asked many questions about the budget. By and large, Canadians support the idea of moderation-which is the theme that runs through this budget-because they are moderate people. Of course, they do not like the idea of paying more for gas and oil. Who would? However, they understand the reasons this has to be done now. This was the attitude of a man who last Saturday told me his gas heating bill will be about $80 more next winter.
Recently, in Toronto, there was an increase in water rates which means the bill will be almost doubled. In addition, there was an increase in municipal taxes. For those who must drive to work because there is no other means of transportation there is the increase in the price of gasoline. All these increases will put a strain on low income families in particular. These are the people who more than ever before will need the income support program that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has been working so hard to produce for those Canadians who are referred to as the working poor. After this budget, the program for the working poor will be more desirable than ever. It must be brought on stream soon.

Like all hon. members, I have followed this debate with interest. There have been many commendable interventions from all sides of the House. I would like to comment on one measure proposed by almost every Conservative member who has spoken so far, namely, that the government should subsidize mortgage rates above 8 per cent to help Canadians buy their own homes. The question that comes to mind is this: Who will benefit from this subsidy? Evidently, it will be the money lender. It is the money lender who will be the great beneficiary of this proposal; he will charge, under such a scheme, any interest rate he pleases-10 per cent, 15 per cent, even 20 per cent. And why not? The sky will be the limit, since the government-that is to say, the taxpayer-will have to pay the difference.
That is what has been coming from the Conservative benches as a solution to high interest rates. I prefer the Liberal approach, whereby the home owner, not the moneylender, is given the subsidy. As a result of this budget we see the subsidy increase from $600 to $1,200- that is, the grant to the home owner under AHOP-and an increase from $600 to $900 for rental accommodation. This approach makes much more sense to me than the Tory proposal.
There are, of course, many other aspects of the budget I should like to speak about, but in the time available to me today I should like to focus attention upon our efforts to bring about the highest possible level of employment in Canada through our labour market policies. If we look at the situation in our country today, we see an impressive arsenal of measures and programs. If we look at the current fiscal year, we find among the better known plans and programs the following: the short-term employment plan known commonly as LIP, which was been allotted $105 million for the current fiscal year. For manpower training, as already announced in the budget, for institutional and job training purposes, a total of $481 million; for mobility programs, $12 million; for special agricultural programs, $4.5 million; for special programs for the disadvantaged, about $20 million; for federal labour-intensive programs, about $10 million.
I am excluding from this list the OFY program because of its particular nature and because I believe it would be better to adjust the school year, the academic year, so that students' summer holidays would coincide with the time when farmers most need manpower, and to use part of the $60 million under OFY for travel and wage subsidies to students who are willing to help farmers, particularly at harvest time. This might enable us to drop the practice- unfavourable, to say the least-of bringing into Canada guest workers who will never have the benefit of drawing from social insurance programs because they will never be landed immigrants and will never have the opportunity to contribute to any worth-while social security program.
I should like to return to my main topic, our manpower policy. Having mentioned those figures and having omitted the OFY figure, I should like to mention one further substantial figure, namely, the amount of benefits which the Unemployment Insurance Commission will pay this year, at present levels of unemployment-a minimum of $3 billion. If we look at these plans and programs as a whole
July 3, 1975

and add their costs together, we reach a total of $3,632 million. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how many permanent jobs could be created with even half this amount? Let me explain. My view is perhaps shared by many members of the House, at least on the Liberal side. It is that Canadians would much prefer to work than to be unemployed and in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. We have now reached the point in the development of our labour market program and insurance plans at which it is clear we have the financial resources available to ensure employment rather than just unemployment as we have done so far.
I believe this objective could be achieved through proper utilization of the unemployment insurance fund by turning the unemployment institution through 180 degrees; by giving it a positive and significant role enabling the unemployed to make a choice within a wider range of options than is presently available to them. The funds administered by this institution-funds accumulated by working Canadians on behalf of non-working Canadians-could be used to pay higher training allowances to those who qualify, they could be used to create jobs in the community, or they could be used to pay unemployment benefits to those who have earned in their lifetime unemployment benefits in proportion to the number of years they have served in the labour force. What the unemployed person choosing to use up unemployment benefits would do while receiving those benefits would be entirely up to him to decide.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to put it in other words. When Canadians become unemployed because of the faulty functioning of our economy, we depend very largely upon the private sector to create jobs. But when the economy does not perform well, the private sector normally finds its role as a job creator greatly reduced or, indeed, completely ineffective. We then turn to unemployment insurance and expect that program to pick up the fall-out. If we were to develop a program of the kind I have just outlined, unemployed Canadians would be given a broader range of options than at present. This would be made possible because working Canadians would pay a weekly premium into a fund which would serve three basic purposes. These would be, offering an unemployed person who qualified for such assistance a higher training allowance; offering an unemployed person work in his or her own community; or offering unemployment insurance benefits, to those who qualify to receive them, in direct relationship to the number of years they have worked-the longer they have worked, the greater their security in the form of unemployment insurance payments.
Thus, there would no longer be a tug-o'-war between the worker on the one side and the officials on the other, the practice of the so-called benefit control officers trying to determine whether a person is available for work, and so on. The proposal I have in mind would remove myriad similar frustrations which presently vex both the unemployed and the officials charged with administering the system. It is fair to say that in 1975 we are ready to begin rationalizing the use of the various support schemes and programs designed in one way or another to assist our people who are not working. But now we have reached the point in the history of the development of Canadian labour market policies where we are ready to offer Canadians wider and more significant options when the private sector fails to provide them with secure jobs.
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
Security of employment is now, more than ever, a deeply felt desire in the heart and mind of every Canadian.
In this budget there are proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act about which I have deep reservations; for instance, the one that would double the waiting period without benefits to employees who are dismissed for misconduct. This involves the question of who will decide what constitutes misconduct. Will this be decided by an official of the Unemployment Insurance Commission? Will it be the employer? Or will it be the employee? Will there be a grievance procedure in factories or in other work places where there is no union? How will this system be handled, and who will decide what is misconduct in the assembly line operation or other working conditions?
Another measure about which I have deep reservations is the proposed amendment dealing with workers aged 65 or over. It seems to me that, as we have always attempted to do in the past, we should avoid any laws or measures which discriminate-in this case because of age. There are people in our society who wish to work because they have the energy and the health to do so, or perhaps a need at home which motivates them, but who are well beyond age 65. These people, regardless of age, should be treated like anybody else in our society. I urge the government to reconsider these two proposals. I am happy about the proposed measures that will take into consideration injured workers and people in training. I only wish this concept could be extended to include groups such as exinmates and in this way facilitate their re-entry into society.
In the time remaining I would like to expand on the idea of the creation of permanent jobs through changing the orientation of unemployment insurance to a system of employment insurance. The experience we have had with the LIP program has shown that the Canadian public values, and is prepared to support, a wide range of meaningful jobs which are in the non-profit category and, therefore, not offered by the private sector. These are jobs that basically have to do with the betterment of the community and the environment. The question is whether we are ready to move from the short-term LIP approach to a permanent program of job creation with better salaries and improved administrative practices.
Let me give a few examples of what could be done through a permanent job program. Such a program could be followed in the field of recycling waste materials, in cleaning-up the environment, in carrying out minor or medium-sized public works, particularly in remote communities-for example, the building of a community hall or the repairing of a wharf. It could be used, as well, in the field of reforestation in certain areas, or the restocking of our seas and lakes; in providing, in our urban centres, services for senior citizens; in work for retarded children and for the handicapped; in services for immigrants; in reducing the pupil-to-teacher ratio in our schools by developing a cadre of teachers' helpers; and in alleviating the pressures in our hospitals by developing therein, also, a cadre of nurses' helpers, and so on.
