The sky is the limit to the innovations that could be introduced if we wanted to create jobs in this sector for which there seems to be a continuous demand since we modestly began testing this new approach back in 1971. Some may ask how many jobs could be created with perhaps half of the almost $4 billion which I mentioned earlier. Even at the rate of $10,000 per job per year-which is well above what is being paid at the present time to LIP workers-200,000 meaningful, needed jobs could be created for 200,000 unemployed people. It seems to me that the substantial infusion of funds announced by the Minister of Finance in the creation of short-term jobs next winter, plus the considerable funds available this year to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, plus the desire on the part of many Canadians to perform meaningful jobs in their communities, are the ingredients that would permit us to move to a new phase of labour market policy.
What I have suggested today represents only a rough sketch of ideas for discussion and deliberation-to shoot holes through, if you like-and is definitely subject to considerable improvement. I submit these suggestions for the consideration of hon. members, with full awareness of the fact that the majority of Canadians do believe in work and believe there are better things to do in life and for our country than being forced into subsidized idleness.

subtopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I decided to take part in the debate on this budget because in the seven years I have been here it is the worst budget of the lot. I consider it a budget with a large measure of immorality, a budget that attacks the sick and the unemployed, a budget that adds more to the burden of the people on low incomes and the small businessman, and a budget that continues to place overreliance on the so-called private sector, particularly in the area of housing. It is a budget that totally ignores our pensioners.
There is not a nickel in it for the old age pensioners, the veterans, or for the retired civil servants and retired RCMP and CNR employees. In any worthwhile attempt to do something about inflation it seems to me that one of the first things a budget should do, and should have done over the last few years, is protect those who are not only suffering because of inflation but are the first victims of it. These are the people on fixed and low incomes. This budget does nothing in that way.
It would be too much to expect the government and the Minister of Finance to include an increase in the old age pension of the magnitude advocated by my party, but even an increase of $25 a month in the basic old age pension would have been proper in this budget. However, not a nickel was included. Some would say that this would be inflationery. I submit it would not. It would help those people who are the first victims of inflation.
The area in which I think the budget is most deficient is housing. It still leaves a major part of the housing program to the tender mercy of the land speculator and the developer in the so-called private sector. This so-called private sector continually since the end of World War II has failed to meet the housing needs of Canadians. It has failed to provide housing at prices Canadians can afford. It has not been able to do the job. I do not know how many more years this mythology will have to be kicked in the
July 3, 1975

face before the Minister of Finance or the government realizes that they can no longer place their reliance on the private sector in the field of housing.
This budget should contain at least an additional $1 billion for housing in the public sector, in which the federal government itself is directly involved, so that land could be acquired and serviced, and so that housing and low rental accommodation could be built. This money could go to the provinces and municipalties, as well as to organizations such as co-operatives which want to become involved in housing.
I submit that this failure is one of the immoral parts of the budget. The whole area of land assembly and land servicing requires massive funding. There must be a massive attack on our housing problems. I submit this would not be inflationary. In fact it would bring about some deflation in respect of housing and rentals.
I recall about three weeks ago visiting a young couple in the south of Regina who lived in a crummy two-bedroom apartment for which they paid a rental of $195 a month. This, of course, may not be considered a high rental in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver. They had saved about $3,000 and thought they had enough money for a down payment on a house. However, when they started inquiring in the housing market they found that they would need two or three times that amount of money merely for a down payment.
They also found, with the kind of interest rate that would apply to a mortgage either through CMHC or a private lender, that they would be faced with a monthly payment of $350 or $450. The take-home pay of the wage-earner in this family was $520 a month. So, here is one example of a young couple who, in spite of all their efforts to save and wait patiently until they thought they could buy a home of their own, now find that they cannot buy one. Also the mother now is forced to go to work. She does not want to, but they have no choice because they have two little children, one just reaching school age. The mother is forced to take employment because the take-home pay of that family will just barely allow them to get by while paying rent for a crummy apartment.
The savings they have acquired for the purpose of buying a home are totally insufficient. Even if they were sufficient for a down payment, with the current interest rates the payments they would have to make per month would eat up three-quarters of the wage-earner's take-home pay. Surely the budget should contain provisions in respect of housing that would allow people of this kind to have a home.
The massive attack that is required with regard to this problem is not something that can take place over night. I agree with that, but a start must be made. It seems to me the budget should contain at least another $1 billion for housing in the public sector. There should also be a target of 400,000 starts in 1975. This could not all be completed because we are part way through the year, but 400,000 should be the target. There should be, on the part of this government and this parliament, some direction with regard to investment.
Mention has been made of subsidized interest rates. My hon. friend who just spoke worried that this would allow
The Budget-Mr. Benjamin
the money lenders to get a rake-off, with the public treasury picking up the difference. Surely with any kind of subsidized interest rate there would be interest controls. I want to submit to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) that his worry about the subsidized interest rate program is totally unwarranted. In fact I submit that his argument is somewhat specious.
Surely we could have a system of interest rates that would favour those on low and middle incomes. Anyone with an income of less than $10,000 or $12,000 a year would pay an interest rate of 7 per cent or 8 per cent. The rate of interest would be geared to their income. Anyone who had an income in excess of $20,000, $25,000, $30,000 or whatever, could afford to pay the going price. This surely would cover the greatest number of people who are in need of rental accommodation, houses, or condominiums. I submit that the subsidized interest rate is a practical, worthwhile and civilized way to make sure that people have something that should be considered by all society as a fundamental right. I refer, of course, to a decent place to live, at a cost the people can afford. I also submit that the only way to accomplish this is through a massive public housing program.
The continual 19th century reliance on the private sector has failed year after year to provide housing. A massive attack on the housing problem would also help the unemployment situation because housing is a labourintensive part of our economy. Our objective should be to create a surplus of housing if we want to bring down housing and rental costs.
With a target of 400,000 starts in a year, and with subsidized interest rates for low and middle income people which bear some relationship to income, we would have a program that would create employment in the forest industry and all ancilliary industries which manufacture the items which go into the construction of apartments and homes. If one were to talk to the lumber workers in Quebec or in British Columbia who are laid off, I think one would find there is unanimous support for an additional $1 billion in this budget for public housing which would be channelled by the federal government through the provinces, the municipalities, and other groups of people who want to become involved in housing. If we really want to do something about unemployment and housing then this is one of the things which should have been contained in the budget.
Do you want to fight unemployment and at the same time do something about our environment? The hon. member for Davenport mentioned this, and I agreed with much of what he said in this regard. Why was there no mention in this budget of the start of a five or ten year program which would require something in the order of $5 million to $10 million, under which every city in this country with a population of more than 10,000 would have a tertiary sewage system installed? This would reduce unemployment and improve our environment. Such a program would capture the imagination of our people and would gain the support of the population.
One can imagine the employment that would be created in the manufacture of this equipment and in the installa-

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Benjamin
tion of it. By the time the system was installed in the last city the equipment in the first city would be worn out, and the whole thing could be started all over again. Unemployment and pollution would be attacked at the same time. This budget should have had a proposal of that nature in it.
I submit that such a program would not be inflationary because much of our domestic inflation is caused by misdirected investment, investment in the wrong kind of priorities. We do not need more high rise office buildings, more shopping centres and hamburger stands. We need a change in priorities and a new direction to our investment. People who have money to invest should be told, "You will get a reasonable return on your investment, but we will tell you where it should go. It will go into projects that are socially desirable and necessary. Such projects will receive a higher priority than do shopping centres and high rise office buildings." Investment should go into such priorities as housing.
The whole concept behind the budget leads me to wonder why the Minister of Finance bothered to bring down the budget because it does nothing for the sick and the old, or for the unemployed. It contains no program that would launch this country into rebuilding and fighting unemployment. There is still a paranoia about inflation which, I submit, is not nearly as serious as unemployment and the recession in which we find ourselves.
I also want to mention something about energy. The Minister of Finance in his budget said, among other things, that it is his hope that the higher tax on gasoline and higher crude oil prices would encourage the use of other modes of transportation. At the outset I said that there were some glaring inconsistencies in the budget. On the one hand it is supposed to encourage the use of other modes of transportation, and on the other hand there is a paragraph in the budget in which it is stated that one of the areas where the government proposes to make cutbacks is the Ministry of Transport.
It seems to me that if you want to do something to encourage the use of other modes of transportation, massive public investment in transportation is necessary. Urban transit, intercity transit, rail and bus transportation, and transportation in the north should be encouraged and developed. This is not the time for a cut-back in the Ministry of Transport, especially when the minister claims that he wishes to encourage people to use other modes of transportation, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) says the transportation policy is in a mess.
I do not know how they can have it both ways. It just means that even if people wanted to use another mode of transport they would find that in many parts of Canada it is not available for them to use. So they have no other choice but to pay these higher costs for driving their cars.
As I suggested, massive investment in transportation should have been proposed in the budget. Also, I find it incredible and inconsistent that while the minister is talking about conserving energy and the need to expand exploration for energy sources of all kinds, he proposes in one of the items in the budget a cut-back in government expenditures on Petro-Can. What I find incredible is that even before legislation on Petro-Can is passed, the government is already cutting back on any expenditures for it.

This tells you something about how much the government believes in real public investment in the development of energy resources, particularly oil and natural gas. It still wishes to rely on the multinational oil corporations to provide us with our energy needs, in spite of the fact that the latter have failed to do so. The minister wants development of and exploration for oil and natural gas, and then proposes cut-backs in the funding of Petro-Can. What a travesty! Again, how can they have it both ways?

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell us when and where you would make cuts.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think this is the time, nor is there an overwhelming necessity for cut-backs. It is not so much how much is being spent but rather where and how it is being spent, I submit. Investment is misdirected and the priorities are wrong, I suggest. The budget should have called for much greater expenditures than it does. I suggest that the income tax law needs some revising so that it would tax people much more fairly than it does now. The minister says he needs revenue. Rather than raising the revenue by imposing a 10 cents a gallon tax which will hit low income people the most, and the people who have no choice but to drive their cars to work, why does the minister not pick up a few hundred million dollars in the deferred taxes owed by the corporations for the last 20 years? If he needs money, and he admits that the 10 cents is to raise revenue-that is the first objective, and the second one is to encourage people to use other modes of transport-there are many other better ways of raising this money.
The federal government will be taking 10 cents a gallon in a special tax; it has already been taking 5 cents a gallon in excise tax, and once the crude oil increase of $1.50 goes into effect, there will be another 5 cents a gallon to pay. For example, the refusal of the Minister of Finance and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to allow all royalties to be deducted as legitimate business expense is continued in the budget. That takes about $700 million a year from the provinces and the oil industry.
The increase in the crude oil price will only return about $40 million a year to Saskatchewan out of a possible $100 million, and $35 million of that will have to go back to the oil companies, which in turn will send it back to Ottawa because their royalties are not deductible as business expenses. So of the $1.50 increase, 35 cents will go back to Ottawa anyway. Saskatchewan will lose a further $25 million in the assessment of the tax equalization formula, which leaves about $40 million for the province and the oil industries in Saskatchewan. I submit that is hardly what you would call an incentive to the exploration for and development of energy in my province, let alone anywhere else in the country.
We still believe in our province that these additional funds should go into an energy security fund to which the federal government and certain of the provinces should contribute. Small independent drilling and exploration companies should be financed from that fund in a massive way under public ownership and control, ta encourage the exploration for and development of oil, natural gas and other energy sources. This budget still runs away from that task. It still places a nineteenth century reliance on
July 3, 1975

the so-called private sector, and it failed here as well. The government has continually failed in this regard.
Canadians are recognized the world over for their expertise in exploration and drilling, in the oil and natural gas industries. Small independent companies have had no choice but to follow the multinationals down to Oklahoma, Texas, the North Sea, Indonesia, Nigeria or somewhere else, though they could and should still be working here. I have talked to some independent drillers. They could not care less whether they are drilling at home for Imperial Oil, the Government of Canada, or the province of Saskatchewan, but the Government of Canada refuses to become involved, and it has set up a tax system designed to prevent something like SaskOil from succeeding. These independents either sit idle in Saskatchewan or Alberta, or they follow the multinationals to some other country; they have had no other choice.
I would like to urge that this budget be substantially amended. Surely hon. members on the government side cannot really believe that this kind of budget is either warranted or necessary, and I hope that hon. members opposite will say some of the things the hon. member for Davenport said, and will state some of the reservations he expressed in the area of the unemployment insurance fund. I hope the government will reconsider what it should be doing and what should be in the budget, get rid of some of the paranoia about inflation, and worry more about people. If it does that, it will receive the support of all hon. members of this House. It will receive the overwhelming support of the people of this country.
At the moment the public is disgusted. The government has only brought forth more cynicism and more of the attitude of "why should I worry; I will just look after myself" from too many Canadians. This is the time to be challenging this country, proposing programs and pressures to the people which will get them excited, and which will meet the needs of our population in housing, transportation, energy, and in our environment. Instead we have a budget which is nothing more than an attack on the sick, the old and the homeless. In too many respects the budget is immoral, and I see no reason for me or any other member of this House to support it.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in opening my comments on the budget I might say that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) would have been much more plausible and believable had he not attempted to impose on the private economy restraints and restrictions-though some are valid and point in the right direction-and if he had followed through with legislative restraints on federal government spending. This is the greatest weakness in the budget. The minister has attempted to give the impression that he, on behalf of the government, is interested in solid budgetary restrictions on government spending, and suggesting that the private sector should also be restricting its spending. On examination the restraint this budget implies on government expenditure is largely an illusion. The taxpayer no doubt will be the last to know.
The minister has discussed cutting back on defence programs while we do not have any new and modern
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
equipment. He also discussed cutting back on non statutory loans, investments and advances. It is very much like the housewife who tells her husband she is saving him money because she did not buy the expensive fur coat or the jewellery she wanted. We are told there will be $100 million in deferrals and cutbacks in transportation, defence, public works, and in many other departments. Then the minister will cut back by deferring contributions to external affairs, industry and the department of the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner).
We should know whether the Export Development Bank will receive a cutback. It seems to be able to loan money to the oil countries at quite a bit less than the oil countries receive on the world market. Will CIDA be cut back? Will the Secretary of State, who has been spending much money transferring people on language courses around the country, be cut back? There will be an estimated $350 million lopped off by withholding funds from Petro-Can, the Federal Business Development Bank, the Federal Monetary Exchange Corporation and the Farm Credit Corporation, but Petro-Can has not even been passed by this House. That the federal government considered it important that it be passed post haste makes a mockery out of the government, and it will do more to reduce investment in our energy resources. This is one baby which should be thrown out with the bath water.
The Federal Business Development Bank indicates that it has not made any loans since the act was passed. The Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation has not been set up, and the Farm Credit Corporation is one corporation where cuts can only be made at considerable risk to our future economy. The minister has said that he will cut another $130 million from planned expenditures of other departments and on limitations on consultant fees, which alone come close to $1 billion and which make the consultant business the fastest growing industry in this country.
The minister also states there will be a 25 per cent salary restriction on the increase in government, but all this seems very doubtful. A headline in the Gazette of Friday, June 27, reads, "Civil Service Likely to Add 6,000 Jobs". Despite the so-called austerity budget, the government had planned to add 9,200 full time positions, for a total of 317,184. This seems to be an illusion of restraint because there are always a number of job vacancies in the government, estimated at 2 per cent. Government departments normally operate at less than their maximum authorized manpower. This is because departments have run short of staffing funds or because they cannot find qualified persons for vacant positions. It is reported that it is a common practice to avoid full staffing and overspending budgets by hiring outside consultants for particular projects, and to use temporary clerical help. There is no apparent indication that the government intends to impose a real employee restriction.
Turning to the make-work programs which are to be extended over two years, of the $450 million which is to be extended, perhaps the $70 million involved in school and job training is constructive. What is doubtful is the $285 million for summer employment and other projects. There seems to be less justification for this. Programs such as these seem to have a multiplying effect on inflationary trends.

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
The 5 per cent tax credit may go a little way in helping the private sector with the investment needed to provide further jobs. I might say that is some improvement in that it is fair, and it has given more sectors in the economy a chance to use it rather than the straight reductions for manufacturing and processing, which were features of other budgets. But here again the 5 per cent is closer to 3 per cent because the manufacturer, farmer, or logger who takes advantage of this section will find his depreciation rate reduced by approximately 2 per cent. All in all, the budget indicates that the Minister of Finance created his illusion of budgetary cuts by merely deferring programs, many of which are of doubtful validity.
Our external relationship with the other countries of the world is most important and this budget does little to improve it. We are facing a deficit of up to $6 billion in our balance of payments. Such a deficit is enormously higher than ever before in this country, even when it was at a much lower level of dollar value.
Adding to the problem is the fact that our current inflation rate is much higher than that of our largest trading partner, the United States. Our rate of increase in wage settlements in manufacturing is running between 50 per cent and 100 per cent more rapidly than last year, depending on the time period selected and what part of the year. The minister has observed that this cannot go on without jeopardizing export trade and employment in Canada.
In other words, our attempt to boost domestic demands and combat unemployment by deficit financing will boomerang, if indeed it has not already done so. The reasons for this are straightforward. Inflation attracts people into the labour force who need to work in order to keep up their standard of living. But this kind of employment can only be maintained by further stimulating the aggregate demand, resulting in more and more inflation. Our rate of inflation, if continued, will price Canadian goods out of world markets and will entail loss of our export markets. The details of the budget hardly seem to scratch the surface of these problems.
From the statement of the Minister of Finance and the government, they would have us believe that the Canadian trade deficit and our competitive position are only problems that have arisen recently. While the specific problems may have just surfaced, their origin is more deep seated and rests with the country, the commodity mix of exports, and with government policies as much as with the sharp down turn of world demand by the so-called third option to Canada-United States relations. The increase of our exports to Europe or Japan has not made any significant change in the mix of our export markets. The Prime Minister's pursuit of the elusive "contractual link" with the European market so far has only resulted in the feeling that resource hungry Europe will have another source of raw materials.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has just come back from Japan, thoroughly rebuffed in his efforts to sell to that country more processed manufactured goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not true.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The United States still purchases over 66 per cent of our trade. Some would suggest that this trade dependence on the United States works to Canada's disadvantage when the United States is in recession. Such a view does not take into account that world output downturn has been general, and in some cases more severe than in the United States. With the world economy growing progressively more interdependent, efforts to diversify may produce no real economic gains, except some elusive sense of sovereignty.
Much of the gain in exports in the last two years has been due to the price explosion for agricultural products, hydrocarbons and raw materials. Petroleum and natural gas doubled from $1.8 billion in 1973 to $3.9 billion in 1974 in spite of the fact that the volume of exports was actually reduced. Exports in agriculture and resource sectors declined in 1974. Farm and fish products were down by almost 25 per cent, and a large proportion of this can be attributed to strikes at various stages of the export system, as we well know from the grain strike of last fall. It seems that failure to settle the strikes last fall meant that Canada exported about 170 million bushels less grain than it might have exported, and some economists have estimated the demurrage costs alone as high as $270 million. It is not likely that these exports will be made up.
The price trend for Canadian products is all upward for 1974. It might be expected that there will be some reduction in price trends in the agriculture and resource industries. In manufactured goods there was an increase in price in the last quarter of 1974 which amounted to an 18 per cent rise. Since the United States purchases over 80 per cent of Canadian manufactured goods, the concern over competitiveness is certainly important. But it is very difficult to come up with a comparison of wage costs between the two countries. Generally speaking, it seems as though the wage differential has narrowed between Canada and the United States. Canadian manufacturing workers will price themselves out of a job if wage demands are too great.
I think, Madam Speaker, this is one area in which statistics could be much more meaningful. The government could supply better comparison statistics than we have had. We have seen the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) quoting from one group of statistics which were refuted by the Minister of Finance, and various economists and labour people have also been getting in on the act. It would help a great deal if the government could improve the quality of its statistics.
There is one area to which the Canadian government must give serious consideration. The automotive trade deficit went from $440 million in 1973 to $1,328 million in 1974. Since 1966 there have been six deficits and three surpluses. The 1974 deficit actually is $440 million more than the 1965 deficit, even allowing for constant dollars. Whether or not the minister is reluctant to open negotiations may stem from his fears, but in fact the government continues to accept this deficit. As has been reported, the deficit this year may reach over $2 billion. I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce should tell us what is in store in regard to the auto pact because almost certainly this cannot continue indefinitely. Exports of petroleum and hydrocarbons were reduced in value in 1974
July 3, 1975

by $901 million compared with what the 1973 volumes would have brought.
This enormous deficit that we have incurred in our foreign trade was to be covered by inflows of capital, but the government has set up a Foreign Investment Review Board which certainly is a considerable disincentive to those who want to invest in Canada. Failing large inflows of capital, we can expect a devalued Canadian dollar, eventual inability to pay for imports we desire and, in the long run, a difficult time for our economy.
I should like to speak about the action of the government in giving notice of termination of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and in placing an administrative ceiling on the Medical Care Insurance Act. This has brought into sharp focus very diametrically opposing views with which the country is not faced. For instance, in introducing the prepaid medical insurance plan, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who was Mr. Pearson's minister of health and welfare, said on July 12, 1966:
... health is not a privilege tied to the state of one's bank account but rather a basic right that should be open to all.
But this fairy tale, this expansive and motherhood attitude to the problems of health care has now fallen to the position that Mr. Enoch Powell, who was minister of health for Great Britain in the MacMillan government, has said:
... medical care must always be rationed. If it is not rationed by the patient's pocketbook, it must be rationed by the patient's entrance into the medical care system, generally at the physician's office or at the hospital door.
The action of the government is a belated recognition that medical and hospital care have no limits in desirable programs, and that the whole of the national economy could be directed for health purposes and still leave certain desirable things untouched. What is of considerable importance in dealing with the Hospital Insurance Act is what the attitude of the federal government will be as to arrangements for carrying this program. Does the government intend to dump the whole of these programs on to the provinces, albeit with suitable carrots through transfer of financial payments? There is much to be said for the proposal that the provinces which are at the moment administering the programs should decide what programs they want and to what extent they will support them. There is bound to be wide variation between the individual priorities of the provinces.
There also has to be recognition that there will be a change in the mix of our population ages. At the present time we need increased care for aged citizens who should be properly integrated into the system. The re-negotiation of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will have to be done with care, and negotiations will need to be long and painstaking.
The actions of the federal government in cutting back contributions under the Medical Care Act will create problems. Inevitably the present system of medical care insurance created excessive demands by patients for services. Whether the blame is to be laid at the feet of the patients or doctors is irrelevant. The act encourages the creation of
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
an excessive supply of doctors in the country, creates excessive expectations on the part of patients, and does little to bring about a proper geographic balance of physicians. Indeed, it encourages physicians to concentrate in certain geographic areas much more than the old system did, under which fees were charged for services.
The government should look hard at its policies for admitting physicians from abroad, and work closely with provincial departments of health and with medical associations, to stabilize the supply of physicians. In most provinces not enough physicians are practising outside the medical plan. This shows that the payment of physicians has been generous enough to keep them abnormally comfortable. The monetary structure under which they work has kept them very comfortably off.
The government's action will force the province to organize their own health facilities. Reluctantly, I believe this is necessary. It has been suggested that this will result in inferior health care, higher premiums, deterent fees and so on. Any system of health care is open to this charge. Indeed there is no assurance that our present system of health care is particularly superior to any other system.
It has been objected that the present system increases the flow of patients to doctors. All patients must be seen, but this does not mean that each patient necessarily receives better care. Nevertheless, although the salary system allows governments to control the money they spend on doctors, it results in patients receiving an inferior level of care.
May I say a few words about proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act? As was obvious to anyone who was involved in studying the act during its setting up-it was obvious to me-the government and its officials had no idea of the eventual cost of the new Unemployment Insurance Act. Nor did they do any real investigation, because I am sure they would not like what they realized they would hear. The old act needed upgrading, but it did not need to be upgraded to the point at which unemployment insurance became an income replacement program.
In the debate I said that the Unemployment Insurance Act would cost us $700 million more than the government had said it would. Those were not my own figures, but were based on figures supplied by competent actuarial people. The government ignored them, and you can see what happened. As I said, the old act needed upgrading. As I recall, the old act provided for payments averaging between 39 per cent and 42 per cent of wages. In rare cases payments were to go as high as 50 per cent of wages in the case of an individual with several dependants. There was an element of welfarism in the old unemployment insurance act but it was biased in favour of the very low income earner.
When the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act are brought forward, we must study them carefully, but unless they are more substantial than the Minister of Finance suggested during the budget address, I doubt if they will do much good. The proposals will come down heavily against those who leave their jobs voluntarily. The act will discriminate heavily against employees who cannot get along with their employers. We still need
7254

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
older people in the work force, even though some think they constitute a problem. When fewer young people, whose birth after the war created a population bulge, enter the work force the services of our older people will be needed; but they are to be turned out of the work force. It is possible that our older citizens will be forced to leave the work force before they reach 65. It should be realized that older people can contribute to the economy. They will be the losers under the government's new proposals.
Not one of the government's proposals will attack the problem of soaring unemployment costs and the many disincentives to return to work. I suggest that providing 66.66 per cent of wages as UIC benefits to an income earner is too much. The payment is too high. It should be scaled down to the neighbourhood of 50 per cent or 55 per cent of wages, particularly if the person is single or a member of a two-income family. High benefits create the necessity for rigid controls and the exclusion of as many claimants as possible] This is done by passing peculiar and unacceptable regulations.
Benefits which are too high make necessary an army of inspectors whose zealousness often leads them to disqualify claimants unfairly. The federal government is changing the rules of the game. It does not want the federal treasury to pick up such a large tab for benefits, so it has introduced an entirely new concept to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is saying that business and workers will have to pay for unemployment benefits themselves when unemployment rates are about 5.5 per cent or less. In other words, 40 per cent more of the pay-out will come from deductions. Increasingly, those working will directly carry those who are not.
The federal treasury will escape much of the burden that it now bears. Indeed, it will escape 40 per cent of its present liability if unemployment reaches, say, 8 per cent. And make no mistake, all indications show that unemployment on this continent will be between 8 per cent and 10 per cent for some years to come. The great danger in making the federal government responsible only when unemployment reaches higher levels is that the federal government will not consider it necessary to deal directly with the unemployed; further, it will not be so anxious to sustain employment. Thus it becomes increasingly important to make sure that payments from the unemployment insurance fund are not so high as to discourage people from seeking work, nor so high as to lead to the appointment of excessive bureaucratic staffs whose function is to limit claims.
Finally, may I turn to the problems of oil and gas pricing. The government made much of the fact that it intended to maintain a two-price oil system indefinitely. This was supposed to be Canada's ace in the hole and would let us live the good life, while our neighbours for years to come suffered by paying excessive energy prices. Yet already one third of the consuming public, the motoring public, is paying world prices, or North American prices, for gas and oil. Soon the commercial, industrial and home heating sector will also be paying this high price.
The two-price system is now in shreds, and we can confidently expect the government to blunder its way up to the world price before many more months have passed. Soon we shall all be paying the high North American

price. This would not be so bad if drilling and exploration were keeping pace with consumption. Exploration and drilling for oil and gas have sunk to their lowest level in years. Government policies have alienated the western provinces. Government tax policies have created animosities on the part of western provinces which will not soon be forgotten.
In addition, government policies have created in the United States the suspicion that Canada is an untrustworthy nation. Indeed, the defence of El Paso and the proposal that Alaskan gas should be moved by pipeline and tankers is based on the charge that Canada is an untrustworthy neighbour. Our neighbours argue that they can avoid trouble if Alaskan gas is wrapped in the American flag, so to speak. Our position, of course, has not been helped by the actions of the Foreign Investment Review Board.
At a time we have run up a trade deficit of between $5 billion and $6 billion, we have managed to price ourselves out of the American market. We did this by imposing the export tax, and now our oil exports to the United States are falling short of our original target by many thousands of barrels a day. The export tax, which was to cushion the price of off-shore oil imported to Quebec and the Mari-times, no longer acts as a cushion. It merely prevents oil moving across the border. The government has transferred the cost of the oil shelter to the back of the travelling motorist, who must now pay an extra ten cents a gallon. Perhaps the motorist would not mind paying the extra tax if he felt any of it would assure his future supply of oil. But no part of this tax will be applied to exploration. The oil industry will not get any of it. The ten cents a gallon tax may have some value as a conservation measure, but I doubt it.
The government has failed badly to organize our energy policies to meet future needs. The Petro-Can bill, which the government claimed was so necessary for the oil industry, is now before parliament, but Petro-Can is included in the list of budget cut-backs. The Minister of Finance said he would cut certain expenditures, and gave the illusion he would shave $1 billion off government spending. Having for days on end sat on the committee considering the Petro-Can bill, I still do not know how Petro-Can is to function. Clearly, the minister himself has no real idea of its function. The government has been greatly negligent in its handling of the energy problem. It should level with the Canadian people, come clean with them as to how high the world price will go, or how high will be the North American price which they must pay.
To do otherwise will be to create uneconomic and inefficient industries that will eventually be exposed to the full energy problem of the world. The export tax should not have been administered to curtail exports to the United States, but should have been geared to allow exports to the extent that we felt desirable. Certainly
200,000	barrels a day at $11 a barrel, which is about what our exports are short of the permissible level, would earn something like $1 billion in this coming year, and would substantially ease the balance of payments deficit.
July 3, 1975

Again, the government failed to come to any terms with the producing provinces, with the result that exploration and development do not proceed. We are today using up gas and oil which was found ten years ago. What are we going to do ten years down the road? All we hear about are grandiose plans that never seem to materialize. The federal government broke faith with the provinces when it unilaterally declared that provincial control of resources is not desirable.
A report in the Globe and Mail of a couple of days ago indicated that the post-budget price rise of western oil shows that the budget is not really satisfying the oil people with regard to more money being available for exploration.
In conclusion, the budget has failed to come to grips with the most important problem facing us, namely, our deficit in balance of payments which will eventually cause us serious problems.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am particularly pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to participate in this budget debate.
Since the beginning of this year I have criss-crossed the country talking with groups of business leaders about this pervasive problem that confronts us, the problem of inflation and its effect on our industrial structure and competitiveness.
I have also had the opportunity, since the beginning of the year, to meet with many senior economic ministers of foreign governments, European, South American, Caribbean and, as recently as last week, Japanese ministers. I have had an opportunity to examine the approaches that their governments have taken to inflation, to observe the performance of their economies during the last 18 months or so and, more particularly, to discuss with them the outlook for the next 18 months.
The outlook of Canadian business leaders can be divided into short-run and long-run concerns. I would like to deal first with the long-run concerns.
One of the worst features of inflation is its effect on investment decisions. Generally speaking, our socialist friends tend to ignore this feature. They focus on inflationary profits rather than on real profits. They forget that only new investment creates additional jobs. They forget that even to sustain the existing level of employment in a factory it is necessary for a company to re-invest its retained earnings, and they forget that, in an inflationary period, new investment which replaces worn out equipment is infinitely more expensive than the original investment. Canadian businessmen understand this simple but basic truth. The Canadian government understands this simple and basic truth, and the budget reflects that understanding.
This is a time to look forward, to remember some of the lessons of the last cycle. This is a time to assist business to finance its future investment. That is why the budget measures with respect to an investment tax credit are important. That is why the budget measures to assist corporations to borrow abroad by removing the withholding tax are important. That is why the changes with respect to resources taxation are important at this time.
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
Let me now take a moment to review some short-term considerations. The future strength and competitiveness of our domestic economy have been seriously impaired by quite short-term considerations on the part of union negotiators. No one can blame them for seeking a fair deal for their workers, but too many groups have sought to make immediate gains at the expense of others. How else does one explain wage settlements of 20 per cent or more in one year?
To project oneself against inflation is reasonable and sensible for any bargaining unit, but when that settlement exceeds the domestic inflationary rate by up to 8 per cent or more, such a settlement itself is inflationary. Such settlements directly and indirectly can undermine the strength of the economy as a whole.
Let me digress for a moment. You are all familiar with the United States experience. Their wage settlement and unit costs have been held down substantially below ours. They did that in Germany also, and Germany had an inflation rate in the last year of just over 6 per cent.
In Japan there were wage settlements in 1974 of 33 per cent. They suddenly realized that their international competitiveness was eroding. This year they settled for 13 per cent.
We should take a good look at the experiences of the United States, Germany, and Japan. In my opinion they are the industrial leaders in this world, the economies which are the most competitive. I suggest we can learn much from their sense of self discipline during an inflationary period, their willingness to face the national interest and to show restraint.
In the balance of my remarks I want to discuss some of the initiatives that my department has taken, new ways of writing new business. I would like to talk a little about some of our new initiatives with our traditional partners, our European and Japanese partners, in connection with establishing new commercial relations. I also want to talk about some of our trade promotion initiatives in the course of this year. But I notice that it is close to six o'clock. I will have to defer those remarks until later.
May I end this part of my speech by saying that, for the longer term, we have to concentrate not only on building the productive capacity of Canada, not only on the scale of longer term, but on assisting the restructuring and modernization of Canadian industry and the development of industry sector strategies. We also have to open up new markets. We have to find new ways of doing business outside Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I would be very pleased to lead a trade mission with hon. members to sell Canadian garments in period fashion, wherever they might like to go.
Before the adjournment for the dinner hour I was able to outline some of my concerns about longer term questions and longer term threats to the Canadian productivity and competitiveness that the inflationary situation in Canada today poses for us. I referred to the restraint that some other countries had shown when it came to settling their wage negotiations, and I referred in particular to Japan.

In Japan in 1974 the average wage settlement was 33 per cent. Earlier this year I think the Japanese took stock of the situation and realized they were going to lose their competitive advantage in the world, or they could see that competitive advantage eroding, and the settlement this year was an average 13 per cent.
I referred to Germany, another of the industrial nations with which we are competing internationally on an active and aggressive basis. I referred to their inflation rate and the kind of discipline they had shown and imposed on themselves in limiting their wage increases and, therefore, increases in unit costs.
I referred as well to the experience in the United States. Hon. members are fully aware of the comparison between increasing wage costs in the United States and in this country. The United States is our major competitor in two ways, both as an exporter in third markets and as a competitor in the Canadian market itself.

speechtext:
I think there is a lesson in this for Canadians, and it is simply that unless our wage settlements abate from last year's level very considerably, all Canadians will pay the price for the lost competition in the Canadian economy.
I began in my remarks to outline what I wanted to cover in the balance of my speech. I wanted to maintain the longer term perspective, and I wanted to indicate where I felt some of the longer term imperatives for Canada lie. I referred in my earlier remarks to our need to increase our investment in an expanded productive capacity. I have referred on other occasions in this House to and have emphasized the importance of restructuring and modernizing Canada's industrial plant on an internationally competitive basis, and to the development of sector strategies where appropriate to this end. The major program in developing these policies with the assistance and full consultation of the private sector is now well advanced.
In the balance of my remarks I want to deal with a third longer term imperative, the development of new export opportunities for Canadians. In my view our future economic success will depend on how well we pursue each of these imperatives in combination one with the other.
Our exports in real terms this year are suffering compared to a year ago because the economies of our major customers are suffering. We cannot expect any major change until the United States economy turns up. I think we have reason to hope that the economic indicators are now signalling that the turn-up is about to occur.
There is not much time to detail all the initiatives we have been taking as a government over the past year to improve the outlook, and lay a firmer foundation for long-term future export performance. However, I intend to summarize some of my department's efforts. I want to talk about three aspects. I want to talk about all the new initiatives we have introduced to support new ways of business; I want to talk about new initiatives in economic co-operation with our major partners; and I want to talk about new initiatives in trade promotion.
July 3, 1975

During the past 18 months there have been several missions of Canadian businessmen to the Middle East, Latin America, and the Pacific rim. Many of these countries are at the takeoff point in programs of rapid industrialization. This has opened up important new opportunities for Canadian firms. Foreign businessmen and governments are interested in more than just Canadian manufactured goods and services. They favour as the best technique of obtaining new technology the joint venture, or some form of partnership. It is a good technique for them and it is also a good technique for Canadians. The joint venture in many instances is the only way of protecting existing markets, expanding into new lines in an existing market, or indeed in some cases it is the only way of penetrating a market for the first time. To promote this vehicle for trade I have established in my department a centre for joint ventures. This centre will be an information bank for Canadian businessmen contemplating joint ventures abroad.
I have also discovered a strong demand for Canadian expertise and capital goods in the form of turnkey projects in developing countries. We estimate the world market for such projects as high as $50 billion annually. Individual turnkey projects range upwards from $25 billion. Thus my department has introduced programs to help Canadian companies pursue such projects. As in the case of joint ventures, I am establishing a centre for turnkey projects in my department. It will provide advice and assistance to Canadian companies pursuing turnkey projects abroad.
In addition to the government's programs, the private insurance industry, encouraged by my department, has introduced unique insurance programs to take some of the sting out of the risk. The Export Development Corporation at my request is setting up special facilities to process applications for financing of turnkey projects where needed.
With regard to the Export Development Corporation we passed legislation earlier this session raising the corporation's ceiling to $5 billion. To date this year the Export Development Corporation has authorized more than $900 million in long-term loans.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the hon. member opposite is so badly informed. I would be very pleased on another occasion to provide him with the information. The Export Development Corporation has approved or extended offers on a further $87 million in medium-term insurance guarantees in support of overseas sales.
Hon. members will recall that just last month we put into place a $500 million EDC financing umbrella, or line or credit, to support Canadian sales of capital goods in the growing Soviet Union market. The hon. member for Crow-
Tile Budget-Mr. Gillespie
foot (Mr. Horner) perhaps should note this because some of the most significant sales which have been made by Canadian firms to the USSR have been made by Canadian firms in Alberta. Earlier we instituted similar credit arrangements for Cuba to the extent of $100 million. Just this afternoon it was my pleasure to participate at the signing of a financing arrangement with the Government of Indonesia which will cover $100 million of Canadian exports; but that is only half of it because the other half will be provided by the private sector, the banking fraternity of Canada and CIDA.
In these three arrangements with the USSR, Cuba, and Indonesia we have noted the response of the private sector financial institutions to our effort to involve them in export financing of Canadian goods and services. These efforts were prompted by the growing demand for EDC financing. With the co-operation of the private sector banks, Canadian exporters have access to credit on terms fully competitive in world markets. As an example, in the Indonesia arrangement EDC has signed for a $100 million commitment. Another $75 million will come from the commercial banks and the remaining $25 million comes from CIDA.
I also hope to announce shortly a national conference on export financing in the Pacific Rim. This conference, with the co-operation of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, will be held in Toronto in early October. It will cover the financial aspects of doing business in the developing countries of the Pacific Rim.
Let me turn now to new initiatives we have taken to develop and strengthen our commercial relations with some of our traditional trading partners, particularly our Japanese trading partner. We are involved with a number of these trading partners separately and, so far as the European community is concerned, collectively as part of the community-the European Economic Community. In an effort to find ways to strengthen economic and industrial co-operation we are seeking to find how our respective objectives can be furthered by each facilitating and encouraging inter-corporate relationships, including joint ventures and exchanges, mutually beneficial investment, scientific and technological exchanges, and mutually advantageous two-way trade flows.
An important objective for Canada in this sort of cooperation, as it is in the GATT negotiations, is to increase the sale of upgraded and fully manufactured goods. A good example of this co-operation is the successful Canada-Japanese ministerial meetings which I attended in Tokyo last week. There we agreed with Japanese ministers to undertake a joint program of economic co-operation. We instructed officials to proceed quickly to identify areas where co-operation would be feasible and mutually beneficial. I feel that this is a significant step forward in developing a closer relationship with this very important trading partner.
We are also exploring industrial co-operation with the EEC and certain of its member states, and other western European countries. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) discussed this in Europe last fall and winter, and more recently a group of Canadian officials visited a number of European countries to identify specific industry sectors where scope exists for developing closer ties.

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
During the past month I reviewed the progress we are making with the French trade minister and the German economics minister when these gentlemen visited Ottawa. The contractual link the government seeks with the common market will provide a framework for industrial co-operation with the community as a whole. I am encouraged to note last week's decision by the EEC Council of Ministers on this subject. It means Canadian and community officials can begin the needed detailed discussions later this year. The progress of the contractual link has moved forward very substantially in recent months. Mr. Speaker, I can understand some hon. members opposite being envious of this performance. A long view and success have not always been part of their experience.
I should now like to turn to some points on trade promotion. We are also expanding, as I indicated, our trade promotion program in our non-traditional markets.
Hon. members opposite obviously do not consider trade a very serious or important subject. In this party and in this government we consider trade to be a priority objective. We are not wedded to some of the old ideas. We are prepared to look at new ways to build trade for Canada. That is why we are prepared to look and to try to develop a community link and a new relationship with Japan. That is why we are setting up centres for joint ventures, a turnkey centre and a whole host of other things. At times I get the impression that hon. members opposite are not interested in trade. They are too preoccupied with other questions.
I have already mentioned the trade missions that I have led to different parts of the world. These have been augmented by a series of non-ministerial missions to many countries. Between here and Japan, for example, there have been 80 missions, either incoming or outgoing in the past year, almost as many missions as there are members opposite.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
