speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Indeed, many more than there are present tonight.
We are taking part in trade fairs in some 60 countries. We are mounting solo exhibitions of Canadian goods and services in many other countries. We are holding in-store promotions, and we are expanding our trade commissioner service in important third world markets.
In the Middle East we have doubled our commercial and economic staff in the past ten months, just as one example. We are achieving results. Since my visit to Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia last April, our exports to these countries have started to move upward by 150 per cent.
There is still a long way to go, but we intend to pursue the potential that is there for Canada and Canadian businessmen. Let us look at another developing market for Canada in the last year, namely, the Latin American market which is just about ready. For years we have been holding out the promise of Latin America, and in the last year, in 1973-74, we nearly doubled our sales to that market, a 93 per cent increase over the previous year.

In recent months Canadian exporters have won a number of important contracts in North Africa, the Middle East, Latin America and South East Asia. These cover a variety of capital equipment and services. At the present time Canadian exporters are bidding on a wide range of projects in these countries, some of them worth hundreds of millions of dollars each. We anticipate important new business from Indonesia, whose president we have the honour of hosting this week.
Next week we have the first meeting of the Canada-Iran Joint Economic Commission. At these meetings my Iranian opposite number and I intend to agree on a list of specific projects for the supply of Canadian equipment and services to Iran. I expect that we will identify projects in resource development, electronics, telecommunications, educational and urban development areas. I think that there is a multibillion dollar potential for Canada and Canadian firms doing business with Iran. I emphasize to you Mr. Speaker, that these government negotiations are of great importance in the development of economic relations, particularly in the Middle East. In this context we will press ahead as soon as possible to conclude negotiations on trade agreements with both Iraq and Saudi Arabia. We also look forward to developing new trade initiatives in a number of other promising areas such as South East Asia.
At the same time our biggest trading partner, the United States, offers some exciting new sales opportunities. One such area is in the market for replacement auto parts. My department is moving to take advantage of this situation, starting this fall with a seminar in Chicago to help Canadian manufacturers sell into this expanding market. There will be 40 Canadian producers at the seminar, during which eight large U.S. importers will present information on merchandising techniques.
We will follow this by an exhibit, sponsored by my department, in the automobile parts and accessories manufacturers' exhibition in Chicago during October. We are also encouraging manufacturers to enter this exhibition under section C of my department's program for export market development. We expect that the Canadian auto parts industry will take advantage of this assistance to expand their sales in the United States.
There are other important sales opportunities in which my department will be assisting Canadian exporters in the U. S. market over the coming months. We will sponsor exhibitions by Canadian companies in trade shows that include agriculture, fisheries and food products, farm, woodworking and oil field machinery, wearing apparel and consumer products, and furniture and boats.
Meanwhile, in Geneva over the next two years we will take active part in the most important multilateral trade negotiations ever held in the world. We will join other countries to promote a freer flow of goods services internationally.
I feel that Canada will derive maximum benefit if we approach and meet these challenges from the basis of a strong economic position. Without this economic strength, we are a straw in the wind of international trade. Thus we must keep the economy steady while we lay the ground work for a major expansion of productive capacity. We must provide a climate for investment, and a framework
July 3, 1975

on which to build this investment for its most productive uses. We must build our strength today in anticipation of new forms of international economic co-operation with the industrialized countries, the rapidly developing nations of the Middle East, Latin America, and the Pacific rim, as well as with the economically less powerful countries of the so called third world.
In concluding let me say that this is a tall order. To some in government and many in business it must look as desperate as trying to perform an appendectomy on a man carrying a piano upstairs. The operation is required, but we cannot ask the patient to hold still.
In these difficult circumstances we must bring the views of informed Canadian businessmen to bear on the making of trade and industrial policy. We are consulting with firms in every major sector. Businessmen have worked closely with me and my officials in our missions. Business views are actively sought to help define the Canadian position in the multilateral trade negotiations through the Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee. There is a continuous flow of people and ideas among the centres of business and government. Indeed, I believe there has never been a more active time, as anyone knows who has tried to book a flight into Ottawa on a Monday or out on a Friday. I believe it is the government's duty to assist the private sector, not to do their job for them. I also believe that Canadian businessmen can compete with the rest. We intend to help them in the variety of ways I have mentioned because, when Canadian businessmen succeed abroad, everybody in Canada gains.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few brief days ago there was, I believe, a sense of expectation across this land, a feeling that somehow in some long overdue way the government was finally on the verge of awakening from its seven years of slumber. There was a feeling that the government was not just about to acknowledge that Canada has been moving down the road to economic disaster but would also bring in a budget that would attempt to face the stark realities of the situation. But budget day, Monday, June 23, 1975, is a date that may well go down in Canadian history as the occasion when the government faced its last great chance for action and when it utterly failed to seize the opportunity.
One thing is certain. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has undoubtedly come very close indeed to gaining his all too obvious wish, namely, the political destruction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who has turned out to be the supposed author of a dismal budget which pleases practically no one and infuriates almost everyone, a budget which offers a little of this, a little of that, and not much of anything at all toward grappling with our economic problems.
While the Prime Minister may giggle with personal glee at his success in finally engineering the destruction of Canada's Anthony Eden, and while the Prime Minister may now feel more secure on his throne from the threat of that anxious would-be heir apparent who has been lurking in the wings since 1968, surely the Prime Minister at the same time should be suffering from severe pangs of conscience for the way both he and his government have
The Budget-Mr. Cossitt
failed the Canadian people, and there are absolutely no legitimate reasons or excuses for this failure.
Last July the government received a majority of seats in this House, but it has replied to that mandate from the people of Canada with another year of bumbling inaction and ineptitude. In any enterprise the tone is set at the top, and government is no exception. If the top is isolated from reality, then inevitably that is the atmosphere which will permeate its way down through the entire apparatus. Obviously such a situation clearly exists in the Government of Canada.
Lavish and luxurious living at public expense at 24 Sussex Drive, with no regard for the pocketbooks of the taxpayers, is an example which is followed by every department in this government. Just as the cost of maintaining the residences of the Prime Minister and his office have risen hundreds of thousands of dollars under the present incumbent, so have the costs of operating each government department risen millions and millions of dollars.
Over the last few years the country has witnessed the unfortunate and ghastly spectacle of a Prime Minister on an uncontrolled personal spending spree from the public purse, followed along by a cabinet which occasionally and paradoxically speaks of restraint while at the same time copying its leader by digging deeply into the public cash register for $3 billion, $4 billion, or $5 billion more. If it were not for the disaster all this will bring to Canada, it would be a funny situation: the captain standing on the bridge saying that all is well and his officers gathered around him in "yes man" adulation, while the ship of state heads full speed for the rocks.
But it is not a funny situation. It is a damned disaster for which the government should rightly be charged with gross negligence.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On the one hand we have the average Canadian facing the inflationary increase in the price of gasoline, which is a necessary commodity of modern life, and on the other hand we have the unreal world of the Prime Minister as he drives around in a choice of two chauffeur driven, $80,000, six miles to the gallon Cadillacs, with the taxpayers of Canada, of course, paying all his gasoline bills.
We have the housewives of Canada continuously struggling with ever rising food prices while the Prime Minister eats in an elegant style which, according to actual government figures, is costing Canadians at least $15,000 this year alone. Perhaps he is even dining by candlelight, since in recent years he has purchased dozens of candles and charged them to the public purse, all this while many elderly people in Canada on fixed incomes can scarcely afford some of the bare essentials required for survival because of galloping inflation.
If ever anything demonstrated how far out of touch the government is with the reality of life in Canada today it is the budget presently being debated in this House. It is a budget which fails to face our economic problems. It is a budget drawn up by a government headed by a Prime

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Cossitt
Minister completely isolated from the problems of the Canadian people.
While average Canadians wonder where they can get the money to build or buy a home, the Prime Minister without any effort whatsoever has spent hundreds of thousands of tax dollars taken from those same average Canadians to remodel and redecorate in extravagant style his publicly owned official residence. Thousands and thousands of dollars worth of the most expensive imported antiques, crystal chandeliers, colour television sets and countless other luxuries have bee'n purchased with public funds for Sussex Drive, and also for Harrington Lake, to please the emperor's palate.
While there are hundreds of thousands in this country who must stay home for their holidays because they cannot afford to travel anywhere, the Prime Minister thinks nothing at all of taking his family at public expense for a Caribbean holiday such as that two weeks basking in the Jamaican sun last winter at a cost of over $11,000 to the taxpayers of Canada.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Against such a background of extravagance, lack of leadership, and uncontrolled government expenditures by all departments-in short, against the background of outright mismanagement of the Canadian economy-it is impossible to give any credibility to the recent ludicrous remarks by the Minister of Finance on the CTV program "Question Period" when he said that the proposed budgetary cut in government expenditures was, and I quote his words, "a posture of self discipline on the part of the government." Even more ridiculous was his statement that the government was trying to set, and again I quote his words, "the climate in leadership and tone for the country." What a leadership, and what a tone it has been.
I am sure that the Canadian people will remember a very widely quoted remark made by the Prime Minister about his own personal wealth when he said, "Let's just say I am a hell of a wealthy man." At the same time I am sure the Canadian people justifiably wonder why a selfdescribed "hell of a wealthy man" cannot set a better example of restraint. If he wants to live lavishly and luxuriously, why does he not pay for his shocking excesses from his own admitted wealth instead of wallowing in the public trough for every last dime? Restraint in spending, so necessary in the fight against inflation, is apparently something only for the people, not for the government, and not for the Prime Minister.
Then, of course, there is the swimming pool, and I would like to devote a moment or two to that subject because it seems to me that it is a perfect example of the trappings of power being more important to the Prime Minister than the use of power to do good things for the people of the country. What is the real story behind the swimming pool at 24 Sussex Drive? That story has yet to be told, and so far the Canadian people have only witnessed a great performance of covering up, of refusing answers to legitimate questions, and of trying to hide what has really happened.
The Prime Minister has asked us to believe that an unknown group of persons, approximately 25 in number,

without anyone whatsoever knowing their identity including the Prime Minister himself, simply out of the kindness and the generosity of their hearts donated almost a quarter of a million dollars so that the Prime Minister can lounge in regal splendour beside his very own Olympic size swimming pool. We are also asked to accept the fact that all this money is being cheerfully given with absolutely no favours expected in return. We are asked to believe that there is absolutely no possibility of conflict of interest improprieties being involved, while at the same time the government and the Prime Minister claim that they do not even know where the money is coming from, and in addition, that no investigation was ever conducted by anyone on behalf of the government into the conflict of interest aspect.
If ever the word baloney suitably applied to anything, it most certainly applies to this entire situation. We are expected to believe that an absolutely unknown group of persons gathered themselves together, put a quarter of a million dollars in a pot, hired a contractor on their own, went on to government property at 24 Sussex Drive, proceeded to blast a huge hole in the ground, and then to construct a swimming pool with no questions asked and with no one whatsoever knowing their identities except, eventually, the clerks who process their income tax returns because of the fat income tax deductions reportedly given them in return for such benevolence to the Prime Minister.
In my opinion the House and the Canadian people have been misled. I cannot accept as fact that neither the Prime Minister nor anyone acting on his behalf, nor anyone at all in government knows the sources from which these funds for the swimming pool have come. I find it equally impossible to accept as fact that construction of this swimming pool has not involved the expenditure of public funds.
Several questions at this point are no doubt appropriate. Why does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) hesitate to tell us what part the surveys and mapping branch of his department has played in the matter? What has been the part played by the National Capital Commission and by the Department of Public Works?
Even more significant, why does the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), or the Prime Minister himself, hesitate to tell us the details of the involvement in this matter by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and in particular the very deep involvement of William Teron, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?
For months I have had a series of questions on the order paper of this House similar to those questions I have just mentioned, and I have no doubt that they have gone unanswered all this time on the direct instructions of the Prime Minister, who is deliberately withholding the whole story from both parliament and the Canadian people in what amounts to a most peculiar and shocking cover-up of what should be a perfectly normal matter under ordinary circumstances.
If there is nothing wrong, if everything is perfectly on the level, if there is no serious conflict of interest, then the

Prime Minister should forthwith issue a complete list of donors along with the amounts donated. Failure to do this can only indicate the possibility of serious improprieties existing, or perhaps it might even indicate that there never really were 25 donors and that the delay in disclosure has been made necessary while such persons as William Teron rush around trying to fill in the holes for the Prime Minister.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Another very appropriate question on this matter is why and how was Herbert Brune Construction Limited selected to build the swimming pool? Were tenders not called, and if they were not, why were they not? Furthermore, by what authority can a contractor be hired by supposedly unknown private interests to build something on government property? And is there perhaps any significance in the fact that Herbert Brune Construction must apparently be on some sort of preferred or select list held by the government and the Liberal Party of Canada?
It is perhaps of some interest to note that Herbert Brune Construction has done quite an amount of contract work for the government since the Prime Minister came to office on April 20, 1968. In particular, this construction company has not only been selected on occasions to be among the chosen few invited to tender on certain government jobs without public advertisements being made, but it has also received 35 contracts without tender calls through work orders issued directly by the Department of Pulbic Works during this same period of time. In actual dollars and cents it has received somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3 million from the government in government business. Such preferred status for this company recalls those well known words that perhaps are appropriate here, "Somebody up there likes me".
What a contrast there is between the swimming pool at Sussex Drive and the one being constructed at the White House. Mystery and hiding of the facts compared with full disclosure. A cost of a quarter of a million dollars here compared to a fourth of that amount in Washington. Money from unknown and unexplained sources here with consequent questionable implications, as compared to a limit of $1,000 on donations, and no money at all to be accepted from business corporations in Washington.
The most important thing is, of course, what the emperor complex at 24 Sussex Drive really indicates. I believe it indicates clearly that Canada under the Prime Minister has been moving very quickly toward a presidential system and away from the parliamentary system of government. The clearest illustration of this fact is shown in the tremendous growth of the size and power of the Privy Council and the Prime Minister's offices since 1968. Along with this has been the tendency for the Prime Minister's staff to usurp the powers and duties of cabinet ministers- Ivan Head, for example, in effect replacing the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) in many ways, and along with this the downgrading of parliament to a point where it has become obvious that the Prime Minister regards it as a rubber stamp to be tolerated only as a constitutional nuisance.
Not long ago the United States found out the dangers of persons working in the office of the president-the Halde-
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
mans and the Ehrlichmans-becoming so powerful that they were making decisions that should have been made by elected representatives of the people. Here in Canada we have the Ivan Heads and the Jack Austins, and it is a sad day for democracy in this country when appointed backroom bureaucrats like these have more power in running this country than the elected representatives who sit in this House.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At a time when Canada desperately needs leadership, the Prime Minister-buffered by the Heads and the Austins-is isolated playing with his toys which the taxpayers have bought him-the antiques, the crystal chandeliers, the Cadillacs and the swimming pool-in that unreal world where the bottomless pit of public funds solves all his own problems and makes him oblivious to those of others.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
True greatness in leadership is invariably accompanied by humbleness in high places. No need is felt to strut about like a Caesar. There is no clutching and grabbing at material things in an attempt to create an aura of power. On the other hand, little people in high places exude small mindedness, a need for reassurance by surrounding themselves with a gaudy and vulgar display of material wealth, along with arrogance and contempt for the democratic process. No amount of weekend helicopter forays into the far reaches of the country at public expense to give the masses the supposed privilege of viewing their Caesar, can hide forever what we as Canadians have in our high places.
Let us hope for the sake of democracy, for the sake of Canada, that miracles are still possible and that it is not too late for new and proper policies to put Canada back on the good road.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
