speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to deal this evening with the specific details of the budget-a budget which I support. I want to look ahead and suggest that given the nature of the Canadian economic dilemma, a different approach to budget making is likely to prove appropriate in the future.
This budget is in the conventional mould. It reflects a belief that the correct approach to economic policy is to use fiscal and monetary instruments to establish the proper over-all context for economic activity. By imposing restraint or injecting stimulus, by expanding or contracting the money supply by expanding or contracting disposable income across the country-as the general situation requires-we guide the economy.
Our approach is, in economic jargon, macro-economic and Keynesian, broad brushed rather than specific, attacking the problems of the economy by over-all measures rather than by intervening at specific points. In a sense it is a method which argues that if we alter the general rules of the economic game we can make the score come out right.

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
There is, I believe a growing conviction that this conventional approach to the design of economic policy and to the design of the budget, is no longer appropriate to Canada's economic situation.
The theoretical justification of the conventional approach makes assumptions in its economic model-assumptions of homogeneity and the easy substitution of factors of production which simply do not apply to our economy. It ignores or minimizes at least four important problems which hinder, and perhaps render impossible, the successful application of Keynesian precepts in the Canadian economy.
The first problem is the lag between the decision to use the instruments of fiscal and monetary policy and the time it takes for those policies to begin to have effect. Because of these time lags, effective intervention depends on accurate forecasting. It is extremely difficult do do this forecasting, and government forecasts have been inaccurate as often as they have been accurate.
The second problem is the very high interdependence of the Canadian economy, both in imports and exports, with other countries. To be fully effective in managing our economy, not only is it necessary for the Canadian government to follow appropriate policies, but it is important that our trading partners follow policies complementary rather than contradictory to our needs. Since they are primarily and understandably concerned with their own economic objectives, such correspondence, if it takes place, is likely to be fortuitous.
The third problem is that the Canadian economy is not homogeneous but regionally diverse-in types of economic activity' in levels of employment and in levels of income. The economic policies which are appropriate for southern Ontario are not likely to be the appropriate ones for the Atlantic provinces.
The fourth problem is that there is not an easy interchangeability in factors of production. Some groups in our economy have positions of power which enable them to isolate themselves against the effects of fiscal and monetary policies. This is, to a large extent, the consequence of specialization within the economy. There are, in economic terms, structural rigidities in the economy, which means that the over-all impact of measures of restraint or expansion is not felt homogeneously.
To be blunt, there are two economies, the one which includes the unskilled, the first-time entrant to the work force, the casual labourer and the person on fixed income, and the economy of those who are protected by labour unions, by professional associations, by the rarity or uniqueness of their skills, or by their management of capital. For this reason the brunt of measures, taken against inflation say may be felt by the unprotected economy, while the inflation-which stems from the purchasing power of those who have power to preserve their purchasing power come what may-continues unabated.
It follows, if these objections to our present methods have weight, that if we are to deal effectively with Canada's economic problems, a different approach is required.

Another way of describing the limits of our present methods is to say that policies of economic stabilization are taking precedence over policies of economic planning. That is reflected by the dominance of the Department of Finance and the extraordinary and unnecessary secrecy in budget formation. The Department of Finance's concern is with the over-all need for stimulus or restraint, with the over-all balance of capital flows and current account. By its mastery of the budget process, it is able to impose budget cuts, or budgetary expansion, on a yearly basis, because of the needs of stabilization policy, even if these cuts or increases are unwarranted in terms of longer term cost-benefit planning. There is often-I should say usually-a conflict between the needs of stabilization policy and the need for effective long-term planning.
I am not arguing that we should abandon stabilization policies. But as I have argued, for a variety of factors, stabilization policy alone is not likely to be successful in managing the Canadian economy. Stabilization must be supplemented by much more precise interventions in the economy. This requires, to use a medical analogy, specific corrective surgery as well as over-all exercise for fitness, a proper diet, and other measures which will lead to good health.
I have examples of what I mean by specific intervention. To show why these specific interventions might be desirable let me place them, first, in a more general context. That context is that we must now-even if unwillingly- come to terms with the limits of growth. The limits of growth do not mean the end of growth; they mean, rather, that we must be much more conscious of the purposes for which we seek growth and that we will face increasingly hard choices between competing needs. The danger is not that we are simply going to run out of essential resources. Our world has enough resources, for instance, in sea water alone.
The limits are, rather, twofold. First, the exploitation of these resources at current levels may well consume more energy and produce more heat in the long term than the ecology of our planet can stand. Second, in the short term, the cost of exploiting the world's resources-because of supply cartels in some cases but, more important, because of escalating marginal costs of exploitation,-will produce cost-push inflationary pressures which will surely diminish and may stagnate the rate of real growth.
Traditionally, as a society, we have regarded growth as the magic wand solution for all our problems. We have regarded the function of a liberal economic system as the satisfaction of the wants, whatever they are, which are put forward by the economic market system. The function of government has been not so much to force difficult and unpleasant choices; its function has been to ensure economic growth so that all wants could be met. Our concern has been to expand supply, not restrain demand. Indeed we have based our economy not merely on satisfying wants, but on expanding and stimulating them. The revolution of rising expectations, which we often say is taking place in the Third World, is most virulent in the industrialized, developed economies spurred on by the communications revolution, by advertising, and by our tendency to conspicuous comparative consumption.
July 3, 1975

We are no longer in the position in which we can allow the continual expansion of supply, without regard to the pressure on resources. We are in the situation in which the limits of growth will impose on us the necessity of carefully scrutinizing our wants. That is to say, we will need to choose carefully among competing needs.
The function of future budgets is very likely to be not the stimulation and the satisfaction of demand; rather, their function will be to limit it, to judge it and to assess the objects of demand. The limits to growth will require a much more extensive strategy of planning than we have contemplated up to the present.
When I speak of restraint of demand, I do not mean simply that an over-riding precept should be to cut back spending in the public sector so that the private sector may grow. It is not true that private sector spending is always socially productive; it is true that public sector spending often is socially productive. There are those who argue that the private sector is essentially creative, that it produces the goods and services society wants and requires, and that government spending is parasitic, and diminishes growth. I think it can be shown that this dichotomy is false. Take an extreme example-the money spent to establish a body rub shop is not nearly as productive as the same amount of money spent to establish a school.
In fact, in this country from its beginning, there has been an active and productive involvement of the state in expenditure, in expenditure designed to stimulate growth, for example, to develop transportation. Expenditure in the public sector can be just as necessary, just as socially productive, as expenditure in the private sector. The true test is not public versus private expenditure; it is whether we prefer investment over consumption.
Looking ahead, we see that Canada has enormous capital needs, some to be met in the private sector, some in the public sector, some by a combination of private and public spending. There are very great needs, for example, for transportation development, for resource exploration and for energy development, to name only a few.
We must, during the next decade, devote more of our resources to investment and less to consumption. We must restrain demand so that we can make the investments required to maintain supply, and ensure productivity. We must diminish our expectations of what our economy can produce for us all now, so that we can maintain a longer term satisfactory economic performance.
In some ways this country, economically, has had an easy time of it since the end of the second world war. Well, the easy days are gone. God has not granted us a dispensation from the world's economic difficulties. We cannot get by with an attitude of, "the good life as usual" in the embattled economic conditions which lie before us.
What should be our objectives, as we look ahead? I suggest they should be (1) restraint of consumer demand, (2) an emphasis on investment, not consumption; (3) an emphasis on improved productivity; (4) support for sectors of the economy in which Canada holds a competitive international advantage; (5) restraint of cost-push inflation; (6) diminished unemployment, by emphasis on investment rather than on consumer stimulation, and by
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
much greater assistance for regional economic development.
I suggested earlier that we should not rely on across-the-board use of fiscal and monetary restraint to achieve our purposes. I said that these instruments must be supplemented by more specific forms of intervention if we are to achieve our goals.
I should now like to give some examples of specific proposals which I think deserve consideration. I give these, not as a coherent or exhaustive list of proposals, not as a complete economic policy, but as examples of measures which could be considered as precise interventions for specific purposes. They all relate to one or other of the six general objectives which I just designated.
I suggest that we must establish distinctions over the use and extension of credit. There are a variety of techniques available to bring banks and lending institutions to follow credit policies more appropriate to our economic objectives. We must insist that they distinguish between investment lending and consumer credit-and encourage the former. We could require limitations on the use of credit cards to discourage the mania for consumer purchases on the "never-never". We should make it clear that we expect the banks to divert their capital to Canada's investment needs rather than current consumption.
Second, I think we should consider seriously, as the House of Commons Committee on Tax Reform recommended, a system of tax integration which would provide to taxpayers a credit for taxes already paid on their behalf, as it were, by the corporations in which they hold shares. As it now is, corporate returns to shareholders are subject to a distorting double taxation, and one which discourages equity ownership. I would suggest that we turn to a form of tax integration for the stimulation of the savings and investment we require.
I think we should look carefully at specific industries within this country to see which of them require long term extensive capital investment and which are internationally competitive. One could look, for example, at the Canadian steel industry which is very efficient, but does now require very considerable investment. We should designate those industrial sectors which require assistance to make sure that they have the kind of capital write-offs which will enable them to expand, and maintain .productivity and competitiveness.
I think we should look very seriously at a scheme of compulsory savings. It is no secret that in our economy we face considerable cost-push inflation as a result not only of wage increases, but of general salary and income increases. The kinds of approach that have been suggested to deal with this problem in the past have proved either unworkable or unacceptable.
In the 1970's the government tried to meet the problem with considered fiscal and monetary restraint to diminish inflationary pressures. The result of that was a trade-off in unemployment which I think was clearly unacceptable to the country. An alternative, the proposal for general wage and price controls, was, I think rightly, rejected by the Canadian electorate. I think, however, that there is another method, that of using the tax system to achieve

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. F. Hamilton
the objective of income restraint. It is in effect to limit by a fixed percentage for all taxpayers the amount of increase of income which is permissible in any one year. Any increase taking place above that fixed percentage would be entered in a compulsory savings account to be returned to the taxpayer either upon retirement or when, in the view of government policy, it is deemed advisable to inject purchasing power into the economy. The result of this would be at the same time to provide needed social capital, to diminish consumer purchasing power within the economy, and to moderate pressures for income increases beyond the percentage set by public policy.
I would suggest that we look at advertising costs in the economy not as an ordinary cost of carrying on business, but as a catalyst for the expansion of consumer demand. The tax treatment of advertising costs should be determined in light of whether it is felt to be desirable to encourage advertising and so stimulate consumer consumption or whether it is wise to diminish it and moderate demand.
I would argue further that we should design a regionally varied tax system. There is some merit in, for instance, a lower level of corporate taxation in disadvantaged areas of the country. Certainly we should give strong consideration to providing more extensive, larger capital write-offs for investment which takes place in slow growth areas of the country. We should also look at the Foreign Investment Review Agency as a means of directing needed investment to slow growth areas.
Lastly, I would suggest that we look carefully at our expenditures on unemployment insurance, the objective of which is to provide employment security, and see whether or not some of those funds would not be more effectively spent in a guaranteed job program, or in the expansion community employment programs, so that what we are guaranteeing is not income but job opportunity.
This is hardly an exhaustive list. I suggest it simply as a set of examples for further examination. Some of them may show defects. I think they are sufficient to illustrate my thesis of the need of a different approach, an approach of specific intervention to complement the overall stabilization policies that we have heretofore followed. My basic thesis is simply this, that in a world in which we have become much more conscious of limitations to growth, government must develop an economic strategy,-a strategy of indicative planning-more precise than in the past to supplement the techniques of stabilization policy.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an article from the June 24 edition of The Times which I think is very appropriate for this occasion. The author talks about the meaningless ritual of government where political considerations override economic ones, and where dozens and dozens of statements are made about the steps the government is taking. These announcements and steps have the ring of absolute authority, but mean absolutely nothing. The article is titled "Taking steps and getting ready to cheer the Emperor's new suit of clothes".
I quote from the article:
-the government, mindful of the interests of the nation, has been taking steps. Steps, that is to say, is what the government has been

taking; or, to put it somewhat differently, what the government has been taking are steps; in other words, taking is what the government has been doing to steps, and what has been taking steps is the government. Here, you might say, were steps, and there the government; the latter took the former, or (for it comes to the same thing, really) the former were taken by the latter. So that's all right. But is it?
That illustrates the logic used by this government.
The article concludes as follows:
I think we are governed by cowards and knaves, who know what must be done but will not do it, and I think that events will do it instead, in frightful circumstances and with frightful consequences. And the government will announce that it is taking steps.
There are many different kinds of steps. I fear that the budget is a real misstep for the great majority of Canadians.
As the leader of my party said, restraint has gone out of the window. The government has increased its own expenditures on a national accounts basis by some 16 per cent during a year in which there will be no growth in the economy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government continue to take the country for a ride, taking more out of the economy than they put into it.
The 10 cents a gallon tax on gasoline will not be used for exploration purposes in a meaningful way, and will place a great burden on people in my area as we have to use private transportation in our wide-open spaces, there being no public transportation. We will, therefore, bear a disproportionate burden of this tax in comparison to others.
I expected the budget to deal with wages and prices. It did not. The whole consensus program of restraint of this government is a farce. As I said before, its own spending is up by 16 per cent. Nothing in this budget will cool wage demands.
Less than a year ago we had a federal election where the need for any radical measures to fight inflation was virtually discredited by members opposite. It is obvious that economic steps are certainly necessary, but they must be part of a coherent policy involving the co-operation of the people. With this budget, the government is losing even more popular support.
Two weeks ago the agricultural committee heard evidence that our western grain industry had lost some $260 million during the past year due to labour demands, demurrage, and renegotiating grain contracts on a falling market because of our inability to deliver; a tragic situation. The government now proposes a western grain stabilization plan, with the federal government putting in some $40 million a year. Absolute nonsense! The money could be better spent in at least half a dozen other areas. Western grain farmers have been ravished by the policies of this government before. They now tell us that they honestly think farmers are consenting once again, and to Bill C-41.
We need a list of priorities for agriculture and the stabilization plan would be well down that list. To encourage young farmers the government should allow them to take up to $5,000 tax free a year that could be credited to a registered retirement savings plan because, in paying off a farm or agricultural enterprise, they are in effect organizing a retirement savings plan. If a citizen, after paying the required taxes during a lifetime, has accumulated assets, there is something basically wrong with taxing again
July 3, 1975

when those assets are disposed of toward the end of that lifetime. Much more use should be made of our tax system to direct the Canadian economy. I see nothing wrong with using the tax system as a means of stabilizing the agricultural industry, for example on a direct, individual pay out basis.
Since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) took office the cost-of living has increased in a 40 month period by more than 32 per cent, and there is nothing in the budget to reverse this dangerous trend. In fact I consider the budget to be inflationary. Our export trade is vital, yet this year we will have a deficit of $4 or $5 billion.
As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said, and I quote:
How can the minister, in all sincerity, talk in terms of hopefully restraining inflation when he has allowed the monetary growth in this country to increase by 46 per cent during the 40 months in which he has been in office-a 46 per cent growth in the basic money supply of the nation compared to a growth in our real product of 16 per cent? Those are the facts. Is it any wonder that during the same period we have experienced 32 per cent inflation?
He further stated, as reported on page 7058 of Hansard:
Income taxes at the personal level in this country have risen a frightening 41 per cent.
The government's proposal to shift the burden of financing the payout of $3.75 billion from the unemployment insurance fund on to those who are working and their employers is a shameful hidden tax. It is the government's responsibility to ensure fuller employment.
The government proposal to put $1.5 billion, free of interest charge, into Petro-Can is really something. If this amount were put out at 10 per cent interest it would return $150 million a year in revenue. This $1.5 billion of free money, if used under the same policy for the Farm Credit Corporation, would mean that farmers across this country could borrow from that corporation interest free. The same, of course, would apply to loans from the business development bank. Instead, we see a cut in the budget of the Farm Credit Corporation to the extent of $20 million, a $40 million cut in the funds available to the Canadian Dairy Commission, and a further cut of $2.5 million in connection with exhibition facilities.
We have the government's bungling and ineptitude where self-styled experts rule in the name of science and efficiency, where we have a high interest policy, high inflation, negative real growth, high unemployment, a $4 billion trade deficit, low housing starts, utter confusion in transportation and no national agricultural program. In fact, Mr. Speaker, no industrialized nation which is an exporter of petroleum and which has the resources we have, has done worse than Canada in the past four years. I defy the government to name one. It is not a pretty picture.
Now I should like to quote from a letter I received from a constituent, a gentleman who, when he retired, thought he had enough to make ends meet, only to find that the government had moved the ends further apart and so he finds himself in serious trouble. He writes:
The Budget-Mr. F. Hamilton
I am very concerned about a few things which are taking place in the nation today, and feel quite certain that there are a great many who share my concerns.
First of all this conversion to the metric system is very disturbing. I believe that this is one of the most costly and unjust things that was ever perpetrated upon the country... We were led to believe at the beginning that the United States was going along with the conversion but from what I've heard this is not so. The U.S.A. is our neighbour and the nation we do the most business with. If conversion does come to pass, most of the people in the mainstream of society today will never totally use it. The only people it won't affect are the children who haven't started to school or who aren't yet born. The farmers of today will never use it as the land is already in sections and will always be figured by acres. Thousands of seed drills and discers will still be in use after the conversion and they already have the acreage setting on them. A similar situation will exist with cars and trucks. There will be thousands still in use with distance measured in miles on the odometers on kilometer marked highways.
It is absolutely foolish to think that it is necessary to convert for the sake of trading with other nations. The people selling our grain convert it to metric tons without upsetting the whole nation ...
There has already been too much money spent on conversion and the expense hasn't even started. I understand that it is already over $700 million. It's not too late to turn back as it wouldn't be the first time that a government has squandered money.
This is all coming out of the taxpayers' pockets and they are already getting a raw deal. This is another grave concern of mine. The income tax is killing us. The personal exemptions have always been too low, but with today's inflation, $1,700 per individual is a joke when you people in government are raising your pay and getting large tax free exemptions. Our exemption should be at least $2,000 each for a man and wife, plus at least $500 per child up to 16 and increased up to as high as $1,000 over 16 when totally dependent.
I farmed all my life and semi-retired in 1968 when I sold my farm. I didn't realize until I sold what a raw deal the wage earner without exemptions of any kind was getting. This applied to me with income tax on my investment income and no source of protection. I resorted to renting some land as a bit of a tax shelter. The farmer is fully justified in being able to write off his expenses, but what about the wage earner? He should also have exemptions such as taxes on his house plus a portion of the upkeep on his house and at least a portion, say a third, of his automobile expenses. Private transportation is a necessity today in a large percentage of cases. For example, take a place like Glidden where there are no services of any kind. We have to drive for everything, including trips at times to Saskatoon for dental and doctor appointments. There is no train or bus service from here and the bus service is such from Kindersley (our trading point) that you would have to stay over in the city to get anything done. The wage earner who can't or doesn't care to own his own home should be able to claim a portion of his rent-say the equivalent of an average of what a home owner could claim-for taxes and a portion of the upkeep.
The purchaser of a home should also be able to claim the interest involved each year in the buying of the property the same as the farmer who can write off all his interest on the purchase of land. To give the wage earner a third of his auto expenses as an exemption you could take away a portion of what the farmer is getting on his car allowance. All of these benefits to the wage earner should be given without any change in the tax structure.
Another big issue is inflation, which government isn't doing anything about. In fact, they are promoting it to some degree to try and avoid a depression. The way I see it, a depression couldn't be much worse than continued inflation. At least everything would come down and we could start all over again. In a period of two years the home which I had some day planned to pay approximately $20,000 for has gone up to $35,000 or $40,000. This is Saskatoon which I'm speaking of, and it is still the lowest of any city.
I'll have to live in Glidden for the rest of my life if I want to enjoy a half decent standard of living at today's inflationary prices. I can still buy the house in Saskatoon but my standard of living will come away down and I'm still five years away from pension and I just don't want to sit around waiting to die. There is no use dwelling on hindsight but if I could have foreseen what was going to happen the past two years, I would have reinvested most of my money back into land three years

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
ago when it was a decent price. I would have at least had something to pass on to my boy who is just 19. Now he will have to work out the rest of his life unless some government does something about helping the people who really need help. I planned on helping him get started on a farm some time in the future if he decided it was what he wanted to do. However, that is impossible now if land and machinery costs stay as they are. The only possible way for a young man would be low cost government loans and have the government buy the land.
The prices for the grain which we experienced in this country the past two years is the worst thing that could have happened. For the 1972-73 crop year we received a total of $1.94% for No. 1 Red Wheat to $2.65 for No. 2 durum. For the 1973-74 crop year the same No. 1 Red brought a total of $4.37% and No. 2 durum brought a total of $6.39%. This is more than the grain is worth. Flax as high as $12 is ridiculous. There is no way a beginner can compete with the bg landowners when it comes to tendering on land today. They have the collateral and easy availability of loans. This price fluctuation has never happened before in all my years of farming ... This has created a situation where land values this spring have shot up to over $300 per acre for the land in this area and with prices for grain going down. The bigger farmers have gone land crazy and it appears to me they are heading for a big bust.
Another thing that bothers me is the bilingual issue. The Liberal government has squandered untold millions of dollars over same and again at the taxpayers' expense. I voted Liberal when Trudeau became head of the party but not since then and never will again as long as he heads the party. I have no quarrel with the French Canadians as a people but leave the French language in Quebec ... The Liberal Party has always used Quebec for political gain and I've heard rumblings that your party was looking for a French Canadian Leader. It's time some party comes to grips with the real issues confronting our nation and do what is right for the betterment of all people ... Just using some of the topics which I've discussed would be a step in the right direction. Beating inflation and a revision of the Income Tax structure, which I brought up, would go a long way towards victory...
My only hope is that you and others in your position will take them seriously.
This is one of a number of letters in the same vein that I have received, Madam Speaker. Although the country's leaders are supposed to be the custodians of the ideals of the nation, I can take great comfort from the fact that the real strength of Canada is in our people and in our Christian homes because that is where the process of character moulding is silently, lovingly, and successfully carried on, and this is where society's long-term goals are safeguarded. Unfortunately, this budget will do very little for those Canadians.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I guess the first thing one notices about the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) tabled last week is that, perhaps for the first time in my memory of budgets, it is a budget that offers no goodies at all for the Canadian people.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are right on.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I listened this afternoon to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), who referred to this as the worst budget he has ever heard, it came to me that this is precisely the attitude of him and his colleagues. They advocate goodies of hundreds of millions of dollars in extra expenditure now; $200 million for this and $500 million for the other. One can see this was not the kind of budget that would be in tune with what the NDP, or at least that hon. member, feels is needed.
But this is not a time for goodies; this is a time for a budget that seriously confronts three urgent problems

facing the Canadian people, namely, the energy problem, the problem of unemployment, and the problem of inflation. The policies that are put forward from all sides of this House so blithely have to be tested by the question: Do they meet the needs of the Canadian economy and of the Canadian people at this time? I support and approve of this budget.
I should like tonight to deal with some of the budget features which are causing the most concern to the people of York Centre. Let me look first at housing. There has been criticism that the increase amounts only to $200 million, and the question is asked, what is $200 million? Of course we would all like to see more than $200 million added to the $1 billion that is already committed for housing in this period, but let us remember that this $200 million increase, when you consider it is to be spent over the six months, is the largest single increase in the expenditures proposed by the Government of Canada. This was one departmental estimate, along with job creation programmes, that was not cut but was allowed to expand, but still in keeping with the requirement for restraint at this time.
I would like to have seen more in the budget for housing, but let us remember that according to the Minister of Finance, we are now spending in taxpayers' money on housing three times the amount that was being spent on housing when the Department of Urban Affairs was set up back in 1969. That is quite an increase; it is the kind of increase that shows the commitment this government has to the important priority of housing.
Let me make another point in respect of spending for housing. I think spending is important. I think the money has to be there. It should also be remembered that money is not the main problem in this area of housing these days. The funds are available. The problem in respect of housing is that the Canadian people cannot afford the cost of the housing being produced in Canada today. If more money were available and more expensive housing of the kind being produced today were built, this would not meet the needs of the Canadian people.
I agree with an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Star on June 21, on the real problem, and I should like to read part of it as follows:
The provincial governments must see to it that the houses get built. They must make the land available, they must speed up the process of approval of developments, they must enforce building codes to assure that the low-cost house is not also a jerry-built house, and they must set zoning standards so that local municipalities cannot block the development of the much-needed housing.
On the part of municipal councils and local ratepayers there may, at first, be some objection to such a massive building program. The provinces, who have the authority, must overrule any objections.
That to me is a big part of the problem today. These are provincial matters. There are bottlenecks, redtape, and standards that require builders and the industry to put up Cadillac type houses when people who are looking for houses can only afford Volkswagen types. We need less red tape and more opportunities for good, basic housing to be built that people can afford. And extra bales of money tossed into the market in one way or another will not bring down the cost of housing.
Let me turn now to the problem of energy. There are certainly no goodies for Ontario in the proposals in respect
July 3, 1975

of energy, at least not in the short run. No one likes to pay an extra 10 cents a gallon as a federally imposed excise tax. Of course nobody likes it. The fact that rebates will be available in respect of any gasoline that is consumed for work, and the fact that the tax will only be borne in areas of personal consumption are very small comfort, and there is a lot of complaint about this.
But why do we have this excise tax? Let us look at the basic facts and at the problems we face as a country.
We are committed, and the Canadian people have indicated that they support the policy of a single price to the consumer for energy across this country. In the west we produce a little more than we need, and in the east we have no production. The east gets its oil from foreign sources, and the world price for oil right now is over $10 a barrel-$10.40 a barrel.
The Canadian people as a whole have been subsidizing the eastern consumers of foreign oil, partly by imposing a tax on surplus western oil which so far has been exported to the United States and sold at world prices. We do not have much of a surplus and we are not able to send south as much as would be required to pay for the entire subsidy to the eastern consumer. That subsidy has to be provided from somewhere. It is a subsidy that will increase further in cost. We are going to need more and more money to pay that subsidy over the years ahead.
What we are sending to the United States at world prices just does not cover that increasing subsidy, so a new source of revenue had to be found for that amount. There is something like a $300 million shortfall this year at present prices, and if world prices go up, as they are projected to do, and if our surplus goes down, as it is projected to do, we are going to need $1.1 billion next year in order to continue to provide that subsidy. The decision taken and proposed to this parliament by the Government of Canada is that the subsidy be funded by an excise tax on personal consumption of gasoline, an excise tax of 10 cents a gallon. It could have chosen an increase in income tax, but such an increase would then have had to be borne by all Canadian taxpayers whether or not they consume gasoline.
It strikes me, and it has appeared to the government, that the fairest possible place to put the tax is on the very people who consume the energy, the travelling public. One does not need to be a genius to recognize that an extra ten cents a gallon on gasoline is inflationary. It is moderated somewhat, it is true, by refunds for commercial use, but it is inflationary. However, it obviously is necessary because somewhere or other that revenue must be raised to maintain the single price for oil in Canada.
There are complaints that this tax is unfair and unjustifiable, but when one looks at it to see who is making gasoline expensive in the province of Ontario I hope people will look at the federal excise tax which has been three cents a gallon, which is now going up to 13 cents a gallon, and compare that with the provincial tax which is now 19 cents a gallon.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who builds the roads and highways?
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not intend to argue that that 19 cents a gallon is a frivolous tax. It may be necessary, but let us realize that it is a bigger ingredient in the high price of gasoline than any federal excise tax people complain so much about. A second aspect of the energy price increase is that the price of domestic oil will go up from $6.50 a barrel to $8. As I have mentioned this is still far below the world price of $10.40 per barrel. We still get cheaper energy, if not as cheap as before, with the proposed increase of $1.50 per barrel. What is the reaction in my province? The Ontario Minister of Energy made his position very clear in the legislature on June 13 when he said:
The Government of Ontario is absolutely opposed to price increases at this time.
It could not be much clearer than that. But I would suggest there is an air of unreality about this Ontario reaction as appears from the very lips of the Ontario Minister of Energy when speaking four days later at York University. After saying there should be no increase he went on, four days later, to say that Ontario energy consumers cannot continue business as usual. He said that energy is too rare, costly, and precious to waste. He said further:
We may prove incapable of managing and controlling the direction of change if we wait until serious energy shortages develop and change is imposed upon us.
Then again he said:
At all costs, we in the western world must reject the kind of thinking in which we tie our hopes for the future to a fleecy cloud in the great, blue sky.
I again quote the provincial Minister of Energy:
The first and obvious one is that the cost of producing energy from thesenon-conventional
-sources may be very much higher than the costs that we tolerate today.
He said again:
A corollary is the capital cost of energy-related facilities, whether it is multi-billion dollar pipelines or the $24 billion in generating facilities proposed by Ontario Hydro between now and 1982.
Later he said:
There are strong arguments against deciding to rely on the world market, and placing ourselves in a position where we have no appeal from that decision.
What does that add up to? Does that not indicate that something must be done to deal with the following problems? How can he ask for a price freeze when he recognizes that we are running out of conventional sources, that the substitutes for conventional sources are very expensive, and that industry needs big capital to bring non-conventional sources on stream?
Let us remember that my province of Ontario would be the first to suffer and would suffer worst if we do not provide for the future and ensure that there is even expensive energy available when there is no alternative. Let us also remember something which I think in fairness Ontario ministers should be reflecting on more often, that is, that even at $8 per barrel energy is still cheaper to Ontario than it is in any other industrialized country in the world.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Plus ten cents a gallon.

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not ten cents a gallon in production; just ten cents a gallon for personal consumption. There is a very big difference. So, if we are looking for an advantage in world trade and in manufacturing in Canada, and are looking to energy for this edge, then we are getting it even at $8 a barrel. We are still giving the manufacturing sector of Ontario and the rest of the country an important economic advantage over world competition. Let us not grumble about it; let us take advantage of it. We have kept for ourselves an advantage; let us use it.
I referred earlier to the taxes imposed on gasoline by the federal government compared to the tax imposed by the consuming province of Ontario. I wish to make another comparison between the take in a producing province by the federal government and by the provincial government. When we look there the contrast is even more remarkable. The producing provinces get over three times as much revenue from every barrel of oil as the federal government. It is a complicated formula and depends somewhat on the price and cost of extraction, but in some cases it is substantially more than three times as much revenue as is received by the federal government. Some people would like to blame the federal government for the high cost of energy, but when we look at the facts we see that it is the provinces which take far more.
Finally, I should like to deal with an issue which to me is one of the most important thrusts of the budget. I refer to the proposal for government restraint. I think this is an extremely important part of the budget. The government has the responsibility to set the example. It must set an example in two ways. First, it must keep the public sector from growing any more rapidly than absolutely necessary in the national interest. Second, it must keep wages within the public sector and other costs from increasing in a way that will signal greater increases in the rest of the economy.
In making sure the government fulfils its two responsibilities I do not think it is only up to the opposition. I have made this point before and intend to continue making it. Every member of parliament represents taxpayers and every member of parliament on whatever side has a prime responsibility to make sure that the expansion of the Government of Canada is kept at this particular time within limits which indicate restraint, and within limits we can defend as being in the public interest. We must watch every increase to make sure the federal government is not setting the pace for inflationary increases elsewhere within the economy.
One area in which big cuts have been proposed is in the unemployment insurance program. I am looking forward to seeing the legislation. During the last budget debate when I had an opportunity to speak I pointed out that I thought quite a lot of fat could come from the unemployment insurance program.
I think quite a lot more can come out of the unemployment insurance program than has been proposed by the government, and I am looking forward to the time when the government's concrete proposals are before us in the form of amendments. I will then be looking for an opportunity to find ways to save even more in that very important but very expensive government program.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part today in the budget debate, one of the most important of all parliamentary events. And yet, paradoxically, on this occasion no specific legislation is actually here before us who have been elected first and foremost as legislators. At budget time we are simply asked to approve in general the budgetary policies of the government.
It is fortunate that the resolution refers to "policies" because in the budget which was presented to us on June 23 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), there is very little of which to approve. I do not mean by this that I do not find anything in the budget that I like; I mean that the budget contains very little of real substance. It is all padding, like the presentation kit which we received from the finance minister's office: five books filled with words and repetitious tables, when the entire budgetary package, on this occasion at least, could have been presented in one book, or possibly two.
My primary feeling about this budget, Mr. Speaker, is one of disappointment. I had such high expectations for this budget, the first major spring budget of this new majority government. This is only the second majority government that we have had in this country in 17 years, and the first in that same period of time which was elected by the Canadian people after due consideration of its probable ability and competence to govern, and not on a wave of some personal mania or other. How disappointed the Canadian people must be today, less than 12 months later; how quickly has the bright, new government of last summer faded, and how soon have the eager expectations of the electorate become dulled.
I think that expectation is the appropriate feeling to mention at this time, Mr. Speaker, because this has been the prevailling feeling with regard to the budgetary performance of the Minister of Finance on this occasion perhaps more than on any other. We were expecting so much; the minister led us to expect so much; indeed, he conditioned us by his stalling and delays. In the late spring the minister told us that a budget would be brought down soon. Then he told us that one would be forthcoming in May. May came and went, and still no budget. The month of June was nearing its end before the new budget was brought down. When one has to wait that long for something, it is usually because it is worth waiting for.
The reasons for the minister's waiting game are not hard to see. Unemployment in Canada has now reached 715,000, a far higher number than anything that we have experienced since the depression, and on a percentage basis it surpasses even the high figure reached during the recessionary period of 1961. The situation with regard to our gross national product, similar to the unemployment situation, is only rivalled by that in the depression-four consecutive quarters of no growth, and an actual decline of 1.45 percent during the first quarter of this year. Our skyrocketing inflation rate has had no rival in recent or in past times. Something clearly had to be done; just what was not at all clear. The disappointment that I spoke of a moment ago is in fact quite inexcusable. On reflection it becomes clear that this miserable budget, this minuscule budget which the finance minister laboured so mightly to
July 3, 1975

bring forth, should have been the expected response of the government to the problems that we are facing.
The budget concerns itself with the financial affairs of our Canadian society; it is a social as well as an economic document. This point has been made before, of course. But primarily this budget was supposed to be an inflation fighting budget. Usually it is not appropriate to criticize something for what it is not rather than for what it is. However, today is one of those occasions when such criticism is justified because of the unique circumstances surrounding the introduction of the budget. This budget was preceded by a prolonged period of time during which the finance minister himself identified and singled out inflation as the number one consideration and the most important problem facing Canadians. But on budget night he flubbed it.
Mandatory prices and incomes controls were of course categorically rejected at such length and with such vehemence that one is almost tempted to quote Shakespeare and say "The gentleman doth protest too much!" The explanation advanced for their rejection was that they would never work because Canadians are not ready to accept them, an assumption that may or may not be correct, and which at any rate is probably irrelevant in so far as their imposition is concerned. Canadians would probably prefer not to have all manner of taxes, tariffs and surcharges either, but that does not make them any less useful, necessary, and perfectly legitimate fiscal techniques.
A voluntary consensus on wage and price guidelines had not been reached either, the finance minister admitted, and in all honesty it must be said that it was not for lack of trying on his part, nor do I think because of any particular intransigence on the part of labour. The search for a voluntary consensus was conducted in such a clumsy fashion, and was weighted so heavily against labour that it was bound to fail. Each of the other remaining options was systematically eliminated on budget night as either "unthinkable" or tending to "provoke administrative nightmares".
The only option finally remaining open to the finance minister was for him to announce in effect that his elusive search for a consensus would continue, and that to set a good example the government would cut spending by $1 billion. Mr. Speaker, many other speakers before me have pointed out what a sham this so called restraint exercise is, so I do not feel that I need to develop it any further, except to say that only the present government could budget for a deficit increase of 177 per cent and then call it an example of restraint. With this budget the Minister of Finance has achieved a consensus that he was not able to achieve after months of consultations. It surely must be the consensus among almost all Canadians that as an anti-inflation document this budget is a miserable failure.
Before concluding my remarks today I would like to say a few things about some of the budgetary policies in the energy and resources fields and the related effects that some of them will have on transportation in Canada.
The 46 per cent taxation rate for petroleum and mining corporations, which will replace the present 50 per cent rate, and the extra 15 point abatement system on January 1 of next year, are a welcome and worthwhile revision.
The Budget-Mr. Masniuk
Combined with the 25 per cent resource allowance deduction these will hopefully remove some of the present confusion in the resource development sector of our economy and spur new development.
Nothing is either black or white, all good or all bad in this fallen, imperfect, but not yet quite completey lost world of ours, Mr. Speaker, and the works and plans of man and the budgets of finance ministers are no exception. The great grey areas of compromise and reconciliation between the black and the white have become almost a Canadian characteristic during the 108 years of our national existence, and this latest financial exercise by the Minister of Finance is characteristically Canadian in this regard.
On the lighter side of the spectrum is the 5 per cent tax credit for oil producers, miners, loggers, farmers and fishermen, for new investment in machinery and equipment. This, too, should hopefully spur capital investment in these vital sectors of our economy. The removal of the 5 per cent sales tax on insulating material is similarly a good measure, and is presumably meant as a conservation measure designed to increase the use of insulating materials in new construction, although whether it will actually achieve this is not exactly clear. The removal of the 5 per cent tax on all building materials, not just those used for insulating, would have been the most obvious response, and is what should have been done as just one of many measures to assist relieve the desperate housing situation in this country.
Next to the budget's worthlessness as an anti-inflationary vehicle, the biggest disappointment is the insignificant help that it provides for the housing industry. The Progressive Conservative party's proposals for housing are well known, so I will not do any more here than just mention them briefly. Some method must be found to alleviate the crushing burden of overly high mortgage interest rates for the individual borrower, and we have suggested that this might be done by permitting the deductibility from income tax of mortgage interest in excess of a certain amount, perhaps 8 per cent, up to a maximum of $1,000 per householder. Some other suggestions which we have made are for tax credits for investment funds which will be used specifically to finance residential mortgages, and low interest and long term loans to municipalities to finance the development of serviced land.
It is with respect to oil and gas pricing that this budget really gets into the great grey area I spoke of earlier. The dilemma of the Minister of Finance is the dilemma of all of us today in an increasingly energy short world. Our smug satisfaction of 18 months ago in knowing that we were at that time the only industrialized country in the western world which was self sufficient in energy has been replaced today by despair.
We have seen our oil imports rise while at the same time we have had to cut back on our exports, or risk the possibility of a severe shortage much sooner than we had expected. The oil import compensation program, which pays eastern Canadian importers a subsidy out of revenue collected from a surcharge on western Canadian oil

July 3, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Masniuk
exporters, has permitted us one domestic oil price in Canada lower than the world price, and has worked as long as exports matched imports, but that is no longer the case. The rise in crude oil and natural gas prices is one aspect of this budget of which I cannot be too critical. Certainly price rises for any commodities which are under priced relative to their value are almost inevitable.
The price of any valuable commodity in short supply is bound to rise. That is logical. It is this budget's 10 cents per gallon excise tax on gasoline used by the private motorist which departs from logic. According to the Minister of Finance, the revenue collected from this excise tax is designed to pay the oil import compensation program deficit, and the tax is also designed as a gasoline conservation measure. It is a most unfair way of doing either. This tax is unfair, not because it is designed to pay the cost of heating the homes of eastern Canadians. After all, if we live in one single, united country and not in a collection of squabbling, semi autonomous states, which sometimes seems to be the case, this is not an unreasonable sacrifice to make. Nor is it unreasonable to ask Canadians to try to conserve on their consumption of gasoline. This tax measure is unfair because it does not give back to the Canadian consumer anything for his sacrifice. There is no fair exchange.
On budget night the Minister of Finance pointed out that the price of gasoline in West Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, Britain, Japan and France ranged from between $1.60 and $2 per gallon. What he failed to mention is that almost every one of these countries has a well developed, highly integrated, fast, efficient and inexpensive national and urban transportation system. What have we in this country? We have a transportation system which has become increasingly inadequate, and there is a total absence of anything in the way of a transportation policy except promises.
In the extreme eastern portion of my constituency of Portage there has developed in the past 10 years, as housing has spread farther and farther beyond the Winnipeg city limits, a suburban or suburban fringe residential corridor extending northward of the metropolitan area. The highways through this corridor have in the past few years become increasingly congested, with the residents of this corridor driving to their jobs in the city in the morning and home in the evening. This tax will hurt these drivers particularly hard and unfairly. These residents have no alternative form of transportation to get to their jobs, and there is no way that they can cut down on their consumption of gasoline as long as they live where they do. Unlike motorists in some other parts of the country, these motorists have no alternative to driving their cars to work, but they might have had if the government had carried through on the election promises of last July.

speechtext:
At that time the government announced that it would soon introduce an urban transit program which, among other things, would pay up to 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles made in Canada and up to 50 per cent of the cost of new stations and platforms, and which would utilize existing track and rights of way as much as possible. What is of interest is that through

this new residential growth corridor I have just mentioned there now exists a railway branch line running from the city of Winnipeg to the town of Arborg, which is now slated for abandonment pending investigation as to its possible future usefulness. The track is already there. Here is an ideal opportunity for a commuter rail service. Here is a genuine chance for the government to give back to the Canadian motorist, who is driving his car of necessity, something in return for the additional burden of substantially higher gasoline costs and help to alleviate the feeling that he has been unfairly had.
Taxes aimed at conserving energy are only fair and are only successful when they are part of an over-all allocation and rationing program which, in turn, is part of a comprehensive prices and incomes policy, which the government eschews. To be worthwhile and equitable as a gasoline conservation measure, any price manipulation must be tied to the development of realistic urban and intercity transportation systems alternative to the use of the private automobile. Without the provision of these alternatives there is no real incentive to rely less on the private automobile, and in our mobile society price alone, without rationing, will not cut down on the mobility which the private automobile has come to mean to most of us.
I would like to conclude my remarks this evening by returning to the resolution which we have been asked to consider in this important debate: that we approve of the budgetary policies of this government. Time and the normal limitations of debate do not permit me to give detailed consideration to every aspect of the budget, and I do not think this is necessarily expected, nor would hon. members desire it.
There are many aspects of the minister's budget of June 23 which are very worthwhile measures, and I have mentioned some of them. Similarly, there are aspects of the budget which I find undesirable. I have mentioned some of those and tried to deal with the two or three about which I am particularly concerned.
In summary I must say that this budget is a small budget. It deals in small ways with many big problems which demand to be dealt with in big ways. This is the fundamental failure of the budget. It is too little, but I am willing to give the minister the benefit of the doubt. Perhaps it will be sufficient, and we shall be O.K. after all. For all our sakes I most sincerely and profoundly hope so. It will give me absolutely no satisfaction at some future time to add to the observation that this budget was too little that it was also too late.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF STOL SERVICE TO TORONTO ISLAND
AIR TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF STOL SERVICE TO TORONTO ISLAND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) whether the government was for or against the recent expression by Air Canada that it would like to operate a STOL service based on the Toronto Island airport. I asked that question because developments are occurring which are of great concern, and because the Department of Transport has very recently announced that it ought to have a far more aggressive posture toward the development of a transportation system for our country. I agree with this new sense of responsibility.
One must start with the fact that we now have developed in Canada, through Canadian technology and with great support of the Canadian taxpayer, a new short take off and landing plane, the Dash 7, which opens the door to the possibility of establishing, for example, in the region of southern Ontario a whole network of STOL service in which small airplanes can carry passengers between such relatively small southern Ontario communities as St. Catherines, London, Owen Sound, Cornwall, Orillia and Sarnia, just to name half a dozen. One could go on and name a dozen and a half.
This kind of system, which I think is highly desirable, should not be considered as a substitute for a railway system. We need better railway systems in Canada. But the communities I have just described will probably never be connectable by a good railway system. They are not going to have the kind of traffic load in the foreseeable future which would justify frequent, reliable and fast service. In other words STOL offers them an opportunity for small volume traffic that is not otherwise available.
In Toronto the logical base for a STOL system is the Toronto Island airport. I do not want to get into the arguments in favour of it, but it is a use that is compatible with all the things that are the highest aspirations of the people of Toronto for the development of their waterfront-for parks, for recreation, for living, for commercial centres, for a great port-the STOL port would fit in with all these uses. The question is how should the potential be handled? I want to urge on the government that it take this matter in hand and give consideration to the kind of base that will create the system of STOL service for southern Ontario that I have described.
The newspaper have reported that some third level carriers are applying to the CTC for permission to run service among some of these communities-some, but not all. I welcome that. I think it is highly desirable that the third level carriers do it. It appears to me, however, that they are doing it on their own initiative and not as part of an over-all plan that will assure that southern Ontario has
Adjournment Debate
the best possible service. I welcome the third level carriers.
I also noticed in the newspapers a few weeks ago that Air Canada wants to establish a STOL service for Toron-to-Ottawa-Montreal based at the STOL port on Toronto island. I oppose this. That triangle is known in the air transportation field as the golden triangle. Today Air Canada loses money on it. But it is the kind of route, the kind of circuit, that is really a dream for an air transport system. I want to suggest that Air Canada not be given the golden triangle for STOL service for those three communities. If Air Canada is given it, it may or may not make money, but whether it does or not, that golden triangle would become part of the economic base of its over-all service.
What I would like to argue is that the golden triangle ought to go to regional carriers and the third level carriers so that it could establish a viable economic base which would make possible the whole of the network that I described among the other communities of southern Ontario. Give it to Air Canada and we lose all of the benefit of the golden triangle for a good regional system; give it to a regional carrier, and the third level carriers and I would say we could really develop an important and useful transportation system for the people of southern Ontario.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF STOL SERVICE TO TORONTO ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I cannot add a great deal to the reply of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) when this question was raised earlier. As the minister indicated, the department's policy is to reach no final conclusions on the desirability of permanent STOL services or on the location of possible future STOL ports until the demonstration service between Ottawa and Montreal has yielded further data. Given that the very purpose of that experiment is to provide much of the essential information to evaluate the merits of STOL, it would make little sense to reach a conclusion while the results remain as incomplete as they are at present.
That is not to imply any doubt about the success of the demonstration project to date. On the contrary, the project has fulfilled all expectations and is yielding valuable data on the technical and economic aspects of STOL operations every day. The point is merely that more of this information is required before a decision on the long run feasibility of STOL operations is taken.
As another consideration, I should also add that it remains far from clear whether the municipal authorities in Toronto would be prepared to see the island airport transformed into a STOL port. Their approval of such a step is indispensable.
Finally, it will be evident from what I have just said that there has also been no decision as yet as to which carriers might eventually be chosen to operate STOL services to and from Toronto. This decision will be taken as part of the government's over-all policy with respect to STOL.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-COST OF PROTECTIVE SERVICES- ALLEGED WARNINGS AGAINST USE OF SECUREX AGENCY AT MONTREAL AIRPORT
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-COST OF PROTECTIVE SERVICES- ALLEGED WARNINGS AGAINST USE OF SECUREX AGENCY AT MONTREAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over one month ago I asked the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), the former Solicitor General, about a Montreal-based company which provides guard protective services. This company, called Securex, had aroused my interest and I considered it my duty to ask certain questions in the House and in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs about it.
I was intrigued because two former RCMP officers, Gilles Brunet and Don McLeery, were part of this organization. They had been dismissed by former RCMP Commissioner Higgett late in 1973 as one of his last official acts.
Because of information I had about certain aspects of the affair, and also because of the increasing use of companies like Securex, and the current problem to do with smuggling, as well as for other reasons, I considered it my duty to investigate further.
Word of my interest reached Messrs. McLeery and Brunet who, together with some associates, came to Ottawa and met me and one of my colleagues. At this meeting these men offered to answer without hesitation all questions we had, and to open their records for inspection in order to set the record straight; for they stated emphatically that considerable harm was being done to them and their company by the impression that some of my questions were creating in the minds of certain people, including those of their clients.
These men said flatly that their company had expertise and competence in their line of work, had always co-operated with and assisted police and other authorities, and they denied that they, or any of them, or their company, Securex, had ever acted in an unlawful or improper fashion. I was impressed by the forthright way these people came forward and, after .listening to them, I thought it my duty to pursue the matter further.
Messrs. McLeery and Brunet are very disillusioned about the way their association with the RCMP was terminated. I suggest that they may have some reason for their opinion and that perhaps an injustice has been done.
Let me assure the former solicitor general and the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) that I have neither evidence, nor reason, on the basis of present information, to justify any concern about the activities of Messrs. McLeery and Brunet, or of Securex. And, since my questions may have created unfair suspicions, I want to set the record straight. I also want the Solicitor General to clear the record, from his point of view.
These men were discharged pursuant to section 173 of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. They were given no proper hearing, in the conventional sense. They were never pronounced to be unsuitable for their jobs. They had many years of experience in a highly technical and demanding branch of the force, which apparently did not entitle them to much consideration. Their case, I suggest strongly, ought to be reviewed by an independent commission, or by some such procedure.

At present the Solicitor General has a lot on his mind. I suggest that, at the first opportunity, he should acquaint himself thoroughly with the background of this affair. I might say, for the record, that I had a chance to speak with him briefly about it this evening. He should find out why these men have never even received their discharge papers after all this time. He should inquire into what special interest, if any, Inspector Belanger of the RCMP has in these men and their company, Securex.
Frankly I feel obligated, as I hope all members of the House feel, to look into all the background of this matter, to discover why Messrs. Brunet and McLeery, who were police officers not without distinction, were dismissed without being given a hearing, without being given an opportunity to answer fully any charges which were the alleged basis for their being forced to give up their careers. The Solicitor General has the authority, the resources and, I am sure, the desire to do the right thing.
I want to make the matter clear by saying, in conclusion, that an injustice may well have been done, an injustice to which I may have contributed by re-opening circumstances which caused those concerned embarrassment. But, having done so, and having stated that I have no evidence to indicate any reason as to why Securex ought to be under suspicion, I ask the Solicitor General to come forward, on his part, and confirm or deny my conclusions, and to give Brunet and McLeery something which it appears they have not received, a chance to vindicate themselves.
I realize that the Solicitor General is somewhat concerned about this matter because, as I understand it he appointed a commission, under distinguished Judge Rene Marin, to look into certain aspects of the RCMP. I would like to commend him for this. I have every confidence that in due course he will look into all of the background of this matter. To do less would not be in the parliamentary and legal traditions that we in this country hold so dear.

Securex was hired by Air Canada on behalf of all carriers at Montreal International Airport in March, 1973, mainly to provide screening security services. At that time there were no security firms in Montreal prepared to take on this job immediately without hiring and training a relatively large number of additional people.
There was some urgency to get a security system set up as quickly as possible, and it was decided to hire Securex without recourse to tenders. No contract with Securex was ever executed because Securex apparently could not entirely agree with one of the clauses in the proposed contract. However, Securex performed well and there was no cause for dissatisfaction.
